questions.loText: Explain potential challenges fund managers face when managing liquidity risk in fixed-income portfolios, including challenges related to data modeling.
questions.question: A fixed-income manager is explaining how dealer market behaviour changed after the Global Financial Crisis. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: Before the crisis most asset managers acted as price takers, requesting quotes from several dealers and accepting the best; afterwards the trend shifted toward being price makers, setting the price they are willing to transact at and then seeking counterparties, which has contributed to thinner secondary markets with lower turnover, wider bid-ask spreads and greater price impact from large transactions.
Before the crisis most asset managers acted as price makers; afterwards they shifted toward being price takers, which deepened secondary markets and narrowed bid-ask spreads.
The shift toward price making has had no measurable effect on secondary market depth, since the same volume is transacted regardless of who initiates the price.
The shift toward price making has reduced the cost of immediacy, because a manager setting his own price is no longer obliged to pay a dealer's spread to transact quickly.

questions.solution:
| Period | Manager behaviour | Market consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Before the GFC | Price takers. Request quotes from several dealers and accept the best. | Dealers supplied immediacy from inventory. |
| After the GFC | Price makers. Set the price at which they are willing to transact, then seek out counterparties at that level. | Thinner secondary markets, characterised by lower turnover and wider bid-ask spreads, and increased price impact of large transactions. Many managers now break large trades into smaller orders to reduce market impact. |

Option (d) inverts the central relation of this section: **the cost of liquidity rises as the need for immediacy increases**, and this effect is further amplified for more complex assets such as structured or specialised fixed-income products. Price making is the choice to give up immediacy in exchange for a better price, which is why managers break large trades into smaller orders. It does not make immediacy cheaper; it means waiting instead of paying.

a.reason: The direction of the shift and all three consequences.

b.reason: Reverses the shift and both consequences. Markets became thinner and spreads wider, not the reverse.

c.reason: Denies the documented effect on turnover and spreads.

d.reason: Inverts the immediacy relation. Price making trades immediacy away rather than obtaining it more cheaply.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b) on the direction, and at (d) on the immediacy relation, with (d) the better distractor because it reasons plausibly from a true premise: a price maker does avoid crossing the spread, and pays instead in execution uncertainty and time. The relation to carry: immediacy costs money, so any option claiming a technique delivers both speed and price improvement is describing something that does not exist in an illiquid market.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain potential challenges fund managers face when managing liquidity risk in fixed-income portfolios, including challenges related to data modeling.
questions.question: A quantitative team is building a liquidity model from FINRA's TRACE data. Which of the following best describes the data limitation they face and the initiatives addressing it?

options.text: Reported trade volumes are capped, with exact volumes shown only below the cap while high-yield trades above USD 1 million and investment-grade trades above USD 5 million are reported only as being above it, creating ambiguity between a USD 6 million and a USD 60 million trade; as of 2025 FINRA provides uncapped volume at CUSIP level with a six-month delay, and MiFID II supplies intraday snapshots for liquid bonds and one-month-lagged data for less liquid ones.

Reported volumes are capped, with high-yield trades above USD 5 million and investment-grade trades above USD 1 million reported only as above the cap, reflecting the greater liquidity of the high-yield market.
TRACE reports prices but not volumes at all, which is why models must infer volume entirely from dealer inventory data.
The volume cap is immaterial because trades above the cap are rare, and in any case models can substitute the cap value itself without material loss of accuracy.

questions.solution:
| Credit class | Cap | Effect above the cap |
|---|---|---|
| High yield | USD 1 million | Reported only as being above the cap. It matters greatly whether the true volume is USD 6 million or USD 60 million, and many models try to infer the actual volume from historical trading patterns, which leads to inaccuracies when future conditions differ from past trends. |
| Investment grade | USD 5 million | (as above) |

The **lower** cap applies to the **less liquid** class, which is the fact option (b) reverses. The logic is protective: in a thinner market, disclosing the exact size of a large trade would expose the participant to being traded against while unwinding, so the threshold above which size is masked is set lower.

| Initiative | Content |
|---|---|
| FINRA, as of 2025 | Continues to apply caps but now provides **uncapped** trading volume at CUSIP level with a **six-month delay**. |
| MiFID II | Detailed intraday snapshots of price and volume for liquid bonds, plus data for less liquid bonds released with a **one-month lag**. Also requires asset managers to report realised transaction costs for European funds. |
| European Commission, under consideration | Further MiFID II amendments including a standardised consolidated tape, a unified data feed aggregating pricing and volume from all trading venues into one standardised source for both equity and fixed-income securities. |

a.reason: Both caps assigned correctly, the ambiguity they create, and both named initiatives with their lags.

b.reason: Exchanges the two caps. The USD 1 million cap applies to high yield and USD 5 million to investment grade, and the justification offered inverts the relative liquidity of the two markets.

c.reason: TRACE provides daily price and volume information; the limitation is the cap, not an absence of volume data.

d.reason: Dismisses the problem the reading identifies as material, and substituting the cap value systematically understates volume for exactly the large trades that determine liquidation capacity.

trap.explanation: WRONG INPUT TWIN at (b), exchanging two thresholds that are easy to hold in the wrong order, with a plausible-sounding liquidity justification attached. The memory hook runs the intuitive way once stated: the riskier, thinner market gets the lower cap, because there is more to protect. SCOPE ERROR at (d), treating a systematic censoring problem as immaterial.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and apply different approaches to model asset liquidity, including an approach to modeling infrequently traded bonds and the t-cost model to calculate transaction costs for corporate bonds.
questions.question: A fund holds a USD 18 million position in a corporate bond. A random forest model estimates that on any given day there is a 30% probability the bond trades, and that conditional on trading, expected volume is USD 5.0 million. Expected volume on no-trade days is zero. The fund assumes a market participation rate of 20%. Which of the following is nearest to the number of days required to liquidate the position?

options.text: 3.6 days
12 days
18 days
60 days

questions.solution:
**Step 1. Convert the two-component model into an expected daily volume.** The infrequent-trading problem is broken into two components: estimating the probability that a trade will occur, and predicting the trade volume if the trade does occur. Assuming expected volume on no-trade days is zero, the unconditional expectation is the product.

$$ADV = P(\text{trade}) \times E[\text{volume} \mid \text{trade}] = 0.30 \times 5.0 = \text{USD } 1.5 \text{ million per day}$$

**Step 2. Apply the participation rate.** The market participation rate reflects the percentage of a security's ADV that can be sold without causing significant market impact.

$$\text{Daily capacity} = \text{participation rate} \times ADV = 0.20 \times 1.5 = \text{USD } 0.30 \text{ million per day}$$

**Step 3. Days to liquidate.**

$$\text{Days} = \frac{\text{trade size}}{\text{participation rate} \times ADV} = \frac{18.0}{0.30} = 60 \text{ days}$$

The magnitude is the point of the exercise. A position that looks modest against the bond's conditional trading volume of USD 5 million takes two trading months to exit once both the trading frequency and the participation constraint are applied.

a.reason: $18.0/5.0 = 3.6$. Both the trade probability and the participation rate were omitted, treating the conditional volume as freely available every day.

b.reason: $18.0/1.5 = 12$. The probability weighting was applied but the participation rate was dropped, which assumes the fund can take 100% of the day's volume.

c.reason: $18.0/(0.20\times5.0) = 18$. The participation rate was applied to the conditional volume rather than to the probability-weighted ADV, so the trade probability was dropped.

d.reason: See working above.

trap.explanation: DROPPED TERM at (a), (b) and (c), each omitting one or both of the two scaling factors, and (c) is the design point because it applies the more visible factor, the participation rate, and discards the one supplied by the model. Structural check: the answer must be larger than $18.0/5.0$ by a factor of $1/(0.30\times0.20)$, which is 16.7, so any option below double digits cannot be right.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and apply different approaches to model asset liquidity, including an approach to modeling infrequently traded bonds and the t-cost model to calculate transaction costs for corporate bonds.
questions.question: Which of the following statements best describes a key challenge in modelling the liquidity risk of infrequently traded fixed-income securities using the days-to-liquidate approach?

options.text: Random forest regression cannot handle large feature sets or missing data.
Trade frequency and volume follow a linear pattern that basic regression can capture.
Bid prices perfectly represent true liquidity conditions, making volume variance irrelevant.
Relying on recent trade volumes can bias estimates because latent liquidity requires additional inference.

questions.solution:
In practice, actual trading volume is usually **lower** than the volume the market could theoretically support. The difference between observable liquidity and this potential capacity is called **latent liquidity**.

| Measure | What it captures |
|---|---|
| Observed ADV | A conservative floor. It records what did trade, not what could have. |
| Dealer inventory information | Posted bids and asks from secondary markets help infer potential tradable volume, though imperfectly for the same reason. |
| Tail estimate, for example the 90th percentile of the ADV distribution | An optimistic estimate of latent liquidity. The framework then quantifies a security's potential liquidity within a range bounded by the optimistic tail estimate and the observed ADV. |

A second consideration is the **variance** in daily observed trading volume. Large fluctuations in actual volume lead to similarly large variations in estimated volume, and where volume variance is high, ADV is a **conservative** measure of liquidity. Historical trading activity is a reasonable guide when a bond trades frequently, but the relationship breaks down when a bond trades only sporadically, in which case data from comparable bonds can help fill the gaps.

a.reason: Reverses the stated rationale for the method. Random forest regression is chosen precisely because it is well suited to handling nonlinearity, missing data and large sets of explanatory variables.

b.reason: If the relationship were linear, a machine learning method would be unnecessary. Nonlinearity is one of the stated reasons for using random forests.

c.reason: Two errors. Dealer bids are an imperfect guide, since actual volume is typically lower than the market could support, and volume variance is explicitly identified as an important consideration rather than an irrelevant one.

d.reason: Observed volumes understate potential capacity, and closing the gap requires inference such as a tail estimate of the ADV distribution.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (a) and (b), both inverting the reasons the method was chosen, and ABSOLUTE-CLAIM TRAP at (c) on "perfectly". A useful cross-check: (a) and (b) are mutually inconsistent, since (b) says the problem is simple enough for basic regression while (a) says the sophisticated method cannot cope. The concept to fix is directional: observed volume is a floor, not an estimate.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and apply different approaches to model asset liquidity, including an approach to modeling infrequently traded bonds and the t-cost model to calculate transaction costs for corporate bonds.
questions.question: When estimating transaction costs using t-cost modelling, why is an intraday, pre-trade benchmark price typically preferred over the previous end-of-day price? The intraday, pre-trade benchmark price:

options.text: reduces benchmark-related noise.
ensures that market impact is zero.
allows bid-ask spreads to be ignored.
eliminates the need to measure implementation shortfall.

questions.solution:
$$\text{Implementation shortfall} = \text{traded price} - \text{pre-trade benchmark price}$$

The primary purpose of t-cost modelling is to estimate **market impact**, measured as the difference between the actual execution price and the order-arrival benchmark or another appropriate pre-trade benchmark.

| Benchmark choice | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Previous end-of-day price | Introduces a sizable return component, because any market-driven price movement between yesterday's close and the time of execution becomes part of the measured cost. A trader executing well into a falling market is penalised for the market's move. |
| Intraday, pre-trade price | Considered best practice. It better reflects prevailing market conditions and is less susceptible to manipulation. |

The noise being removed is therefore **market return**, not measurement error in the usual sense. Because fixed-income markets often lack transparent and timely pricing, estimates are already noisy, and measurement error must be considered, especially where the potential error is large relative to the value being measured.

a.reason: Removing the overnight return component reduces benchmark-related noise, and the intraday price is also less open to manipulation.

b.reason: Reverses the purpose. The benchmark is chosen so that market impact can be measured accurately, not so that it becomes zero. A benchmark that made impact zero would measure nothing.

c.reason: Bid-ask spreads are a component of fixed costs within the t-cost model and are not eliminated by the choice of benchmark.

d.reason: Implementation shortfall is the measure being computed, so a better benchmark improves it rather than removing the need for it.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP at (b) between measuring a quantity and eliminating it, which is the most common misreading of any benchmark question. SCOPE ERROR at (c) and (d), each claiming the benchmark choice removes a component of the model that it does not touch. The one-line test: a benchmark is a reference point, so it can only change what a measurement is relative to, never whether the underlying cost exists.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and apply different approaches to model asset liquidity, including an approach to modeling infrequently traded bonds and the t-cost model to calculate transaction costs for corporate bonds.
questions.question: A quantitative team is specifying a t-cost model for corporate bonds. Which of the following best describes its structure and estimation?

options.text: The model has two components, the first capturing fixed costs such as commissions and bid-ask spreads and the second estimating realised market impact costs which reflect how position size affects execution; it uses intraday benchmark prices, empirical transaction data and bond-specific attributes, with regression techniques applied to estimate certain components and observations weighted by dollar amount traded.
The model has a single component capturing total cost as a fixed percentage of notional, since separating fixed from variable costs is not possible with fixed-income data.

The model has two components, the first capturing market impact and the second capturing the return earned between order arrival and execution, which is added to the cost estimate to give a total economic cost.

The model has two components as in (a), but observations should be weighted equally rather than by dollar amount, since weighting by size would allow a small number of block trades to dominate the estimate.

questions.solution:
| Component | Content |
|---|---|
| First: fixed costs | Commissions and bid-ask spreads. The bid-ask spread can be normalised by the mid-price of benchmark quotes, though comparability across bonds becomes less reliable when the securities trade infrequently. |
| Second: market impact | Realised market impact costs, reflecting how position size affects execution costs. This is the component the model primarily exists to estimate. |

| Estimation input or choice | Rationale |
|---|---|
| Intraday benchmark prices, empirical transaction data, bond-specific attributes | The three named inputs used to forecast both fixed and market impact costs. |
| Weight observations by dollar amount traded | Accounts for the large number of small, odd-lot trades, which would otherwise dominate an equally weighted regression and understate the costs that matter for institutional-size execution. |
| Use a cohort of similar securities where a bond has limited data | Cohorts can be built from option-adjusted spread, duration, yield or bid-ask spread; machine learning methods including clustering, tree-based models and neural networks can assist. |

Option (d) inverts the weighting rationale: the concern is not that block trades dominate but that **odd lots** do, since fixed-income trade counts are overwhelmingly small trades.

**Scope note, flagged under Section 0.** The standard functional form of the t-cost model appears in Book 5 as an image and is not reproduced in the text available in project knowledge. This document therefore describes the model's two-component structure and its estimation, both of which are stated in words, and does not assert a specific parameterisation. Verify the equation against the GARP original before attempting a computational question on it.

a.reason: Both components, the three inputs, the regression technique and the dollar-weighting convention.

b.reason: The model explicitly separates fixed costs from market impact, and it is the second component that carries the size dependence the model exists to capture.

c.reason: Adds a return component to the cost estimate, which is precisely the defect that using the previous end-of-day benchmark introduces and that Q50 identifies as the reason for preferring an intraday benchmark.

d.reason: Reverses the weighting rationale. Dollar weighting is applied to prevent small odd-lot trades from dominating, not to prevent block trades from doing so.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (d) on the weighting rationale, and it is well built because the concern it names, that a few large observations distort a regression, is a legitimate general worry. Here the distribution runs the other way. SIBLING SWAP at (c), importing the end-of-day benchmark defect as though it were a design feature.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests.
questions.question: A U.S.-based '40 Act fund faces redemption requests exceeding its cash holdings. Which of the following describes the redemption waterfall correctly?

options.text: Layer 1 is cash and highly liquid assets; Layer 2 is pro rata or risk-constant asset sales, taking care that the remaining portfolio maintains approximately the same risk profile as before the redemptions; Layer 3 is short-term borrowings such as reverse repos, overdraft facilities or lines of credit, subject to a limit restricting borrowing to no more than 33.3% of total fund assets.
Layer 1 is short-term borrowing, since drawing a credit line avoids crystallising losses; Layer 2 is cash; Layer 3 is asset sales, used only when borrowing capacity is exhausted.

Layer 1 is cash; Layer 2 is the sale of the least liquid holdings first, which preserves the liquid buffer for future redemptions; Layer 3 is short-term borrowing, which is unlimited for '40 Act funds.

Layer 1 is cash; Layer 2 is asset sales concentrated in the most liquid holdings, which necessarily leaves the remaining portfolio less liquid but preserves its risk profile; Layer 3 is short-term borrowing capped at 50% of total fund assets.

questions.solution:
| Layer | Source | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cash and highly liquid assets | Used for meeting routine or unplanned redemption noise while minimising transaction costs; supporting a derivatives overlay strategy; or responding strategically to market conditions. |
| 2 | Pro rata or risk-constant asset sales | Where requests exceed Layer 1, less liquid holdings may need to be sold. Care must be taken to ensure the remaining portfolio maintains **approximately the same risk profile** as before the redemptions. |
| 3 | Short-term borrowings | A final option: reverse repos, overdraft facilities or lines of credit. '40 Act funds are subject to a limit restricting borrowing to **no more than 33.3%** of total fund assets. |

The ordering follows cost: cash is free to deploy, asset sales cost transaction costs and market impact, and borrowing costs interest and consumes a facility that may be needed later.

The Layer 2 requirement deserves emphasis: selling the most liquid holdings is cheapest today and leaves remaining shareholders with a progressively more illiquid portfolio, which is exactly the outcome the framework's guiding objective in LO 18 forbids. Selling the least liquid holdings first, as option (c) proposes, maximises transaction costs and market impact at the worst moment.

a.reason: All three layers in order, with the risk-constant requirement and the 33.3% limit.

b.reason: Inverts the ordering entirely, placing the most expensive and most constrained source first.

c.reason: Reverses the Layer 2 principle and removes the borrowing limit. Borrowing by '40 Act funds is capped at 33.3% of total assets.

d.reason: Concentrating sales in the most liquid holdings is the opposite of risk-constant, and it is the behaviour that leaves remaining shareholders with an illiquid portfolio. The 50% cap is also wrong.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (c) and (d) on which holdings to sell, which is the substantive judgment in this LO: neither the most nor the least liquid, but a proportionate slice that leaves the risk profile intact. WRONG INPUT TWIN at (d) on the borrowing cap. Note that (d) contains an internal contradiction worth spotting, since selling the most liquid holdings cannot both leave the portfolio less liquid and preserve its risk profile.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests.
questions.question: An analyst is applying the historical redemption-at-risk model to estimate potential redemption demand. Which of the following is LEAST likely to represent a key challenge of this approach?

options.text: Some funds may lack sufficient redemption history because they are new or have been growing rapidly.
Limited transparency between asset managers and end investors can reduce the quality of available data.
Investor withdrawal behaviour may be driven by idiosyncratic factors that are difficult to model statistically.
Historical data provides a stable and reliable indicator of future redemption pressures across all market environments.

questions.solution:
In an ideal setting, analysts could estimate worst-case outflows from historical fund flows, such as the **99th-percentile, five-day redemption scenario** over the life of the fund. That is the basis of the historical redemption-at-risk (HRaR) model.

| Challenge | Content |
|---|---|
| Insufficient history | Some funds may not have experienced meaningful outflows because they are either new or still in a rapid growth phase. |
| Unmodellable behaviour | Fund redemptions may be driven by idiosyncratic investor behaviour that cannot be modelled reliably. |
| Visibility | Some asset managers lack granular visibility into who is submitting redemption requests, because a third party such as a custodian operates between the fund and the end investor. |

Statement (d) asserts the reliability that all three challenges deny, and the absolute qualifier "across all market environments" is the tell. Large outflows typically arise from a combination of systemic and idiosyncratic factors: systemic influences include sector-wide disruptions and macroeconomic shocks, while idiosyncratic factors include investor behaviour, peer fund performance, discretionary cash flow needs and event-driven risks.

a.reason: The first named challenge. Not the exception.

b.reason: The third named challenge, arising from custodian intermediation. Not the exception.

c.reason: The second named challenge. Not the exception.

d.reason: Contradicts all three challenges and is the premise the model's critics reject. This is the exception.

trap.explanation: ABSOLUTE-CLAIM TRAP at (d), and this item is a clean illustration of the asymmetry noted throughout the blueprint: three hedged statements describing limitations and one confident statement asserting reliability. Under a least-likely qualifier the confident option is almost always the answer, and here the phrase doing the damage is "across all market environments", since the model's whole difficulty is that stressed environments differ from the sampled history.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests.
questions.question: A fund frames its liquidation schedule as an optimisation problem. Which of the following constraints is NOT among those the reading describes?

options.text: A required liquidation amount over a specified period, for example USD 200 million within two days.
A sector capacity constraint recognising that large, simultaneous sales of similar fixed-income securities can quickly exhaust the market's ability to absorb additional supply.
A time-lag constraint in days for strategies with fixed time constraints such as IPO lockups.
A constraint requiring that the fund's realised transaction costs be reported to investors within one month of each liquidation event.

questions.solution:
Fund liquidity management can be framed as an optimisation in which managers balance liquidity, transaction costs and portfolio risk while meeting redemption obligations.

| Constraint | Content |
|---|---|
| Redemption obligation | Actual or expected obligations enter as a required liquidation amount over a specified period, for example USD 200 million within two days. |
| ADV and participation rate | Where security $i$ has an ADV and belongs to a sector with an assigned participation rate, the daily sale is bounded accordingly. |
| Sector capacity | Large, simultaneous sales of similar fixed-income securities can quickly exhaust the market's ability to absorb additional supply. |
| Time lag | Some strategies have fixed time constraints such as IPO lockups, handled through a time-lag constraint measured in days. |
| Risk | Well-managed portfolios remain below a specified risk threshold, such as tracking error for an index fund. |

Option (d) describes a **disclosure obligation**. MiFID II does require asset managers to report realised transaction costs for European funds, which is why the statement sounds familiar, but that is a transparency initiative discussed under LO 19, not a constraint inside the optimisation.

a.reason: A named constraint, with the source's own USD 200 million example. Not the exception.

b.reason: A named constraint, addressing sector-level absorption capacity. Not the exception.

c.reason: A named constraint, with IPO lockups as the example. Not the exception.

d.reason: A reporting requirement rather than an optimisation constraint. It affects what is disclosed after the fact, not what may be sold. This is the exception.

trap.explanation: SCOPE ERROR at (d), importing a genuine requirement from a different part of the same reading, which is the hardest form of this operator because the fact itself is true and the candidate's recognition of it works against them. The structural test: an optimisation constraint must bind a decision variable, here how much of each security to sell on each day. A reporting deadline does not.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.
questions.question: A consultant is explaining the Geltner-Ross-Zisler unsmoothing process to a trustee board. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: Unsmoothing is a filtering problem, but unlike standard filtering which removes noise, it adds noise back to reported returns to uncover the true, noisier returns; the observed series is modelled as an AR(1) process and inverted, and if the assumed transfer function is right the resulting series should have zero autocorrelation.
Unsmoothing is a standard filtering problem that removes noise from reported returns, revealing an underlying signal that is less volatile than the reported series.

Unsmoothing replaces reported returns with the returns of a comparable listed proxy, since the true returns of an illiquid asset are unobservable and cannot be recovered from the reported series alone.
Unsmoothing adds noise back to reported returns, and the resulting true series should exhibit higher autocorrelation than the observed series, confirming that the smoothing has been reversed.

questions.solution:
The analogy in the source is a mobile phone call on a freeway. The full transmission contains both signal and noise, so the true signal is **less** volatile than the full transmission. Standard filtering removes noise. **The key difference is that unsmoothing adds noise back** to the reported returns to uncover the true returns.

| Element | Content |
|---|---|
| Observation equation | Observed returns follow an AR(1) process with autocorrelation parameter $\varphi$, less than one in absolute value. |
| The filter, Equation 19.2 | The relation is inverted to recover true returns from observed ones. |
| Diagnostic | If the assumption on the transfer function is right, the returns implied by the filter should have **zero autocorrelation**. The filter takes an autocorrelated series of observed returns and produces true returns close to IID, meaning not forecastable. |

Option (d) reverses the diagnostic. Smoothing is what **creates** autocorrelation, so removing the smoothing must remove the autocorrelation rather than increase it.

The related literature is worth knowing by name. Geltner (1991) and Ross and Zisler (1991) developed the first algorithms; Geltner estimates that betas are understated by a factor of 0.5 for real estate returns, a **population problem** rather than a small-sample problem.

a.reason: The reversal of standard filtering, the AR(1) structure, and the zero-autocorrelation diagnostic.

b.reason: Describes standard filtering, which is precisely what the source contrasts unsmoothing against. The true series is more volatile than the reported one, not less.

c.reason: Substitutes a proxy approach. The true returns are recoverable from the reported series given the autocorrelation parameter, which is the point of Equation 19.2.

d.reason: Correct on the first clause, then reverses the diagnostic. Successful unsmoothing removes autocorrelation.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b) on the direction of the filter and at (d) on the autocorrelation diagnostic, with (d) the better build because its first clause is verbatim correct. The chain to hold: smoothing creates autocorrelation and suppresses variance, so unsmoothing removes autocorrelation and restores variance.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.
questions.question: Equation 19.3 of the Geltner-Ross-Zisler framework relates the variance of true returns to the variance of observed returns through the autocorrelation parameter phi. Which of the following describes its behaviour correctly?

options.text: $var(r) = \left[\dfrac{1+\varphi^2}{1-\varphi^2}\right]\cdot var(r^*)$, so the true variance is always at least as large as the observed variance, and the understatement widens as $\varphi$ rises toward one.
$var(r) = \left[\dfrac{1-\varphi^2}{1+\varphi^2}\right]\cdot var(r^*)$, so the true variance is always smaller than the observed variance, reflecting the removal of measurement noise.

$var(r) = \left[\dfrac{1+\varphi^2}{1-\varphi^2}\right]\cdot var(r^*)$, so the true variance exceeds the observed variance, but only when $\varphi$ is negative; positive autocorrelation leaves variance unchanged.

The relation depends on the sign of $\varphi$ rather than its magnitude, so an illiquid asset with strongly negative autocorrelation would have its risk overstated rather than understated by the reported series.

questions.solution:
$$var(r_t) = \left[\frac{1+\varphi^2}{1-\varphi^2}\right]\cdot var(r^*_t) \geq var(r^*_t)$$

where $r$ is the true, unobservable return and $r^*$ the reported, observable return.

| $\varphi$ | Variance multiplier | Volatility multiplier | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.0 | 1.00 | 1.00 | No smoothing; reported equals true. |
| 0.3 | 1.20 | 1.09 | Mild understatement. |
| 0.5 | 1.67 | 1.29 | Volatility understated by roughly 22%. |
| 0.8 | 4.56 | 2.13 | Reported volatility is less than half the truth. |

Three properties follow directly. The multiplier is **at least one**, so reported risk can only understate. It depends on $\varphi^2$, so **the sign is irrelevant** and only the magnitude matters. And it rises without bound as $|\varphi|$ approaches one.

Ang's simulated illustration gives the same conclusion empirically: quarterly-sampled volatility of 0.23 against 0.28 computed from overlapping daily data on the identical price path, an understatement of about 18%.

a.reason: The relation, the bound, and the correct behaviour as phi rises.

b.reason: Inverts the ratio, which would make true variance smaller than reported and would describe standard noise removal rather than unsmoothing.

c.reason: Correct relation, then adds a sign condition that the squaring removes. Positive autocorrelation is in fact the empirically relevant case for illiquid assets.

d.reason: Reverses the roles of sign and magnitude. Only the magnitude matters, and the reported series understates risk regardless of sign.

trap.explanation: SIGN ERROR at (b) in the form of an inverted ratio, and SCOPE ERROR at (c) and (d), each attaching a sign condition to a squared parameter. The check that settles all three without algebra: the entire purpose of unsmoothing is to restore variance, so any relation producing a multiplier below one is describing the wrong operation. Then confirm that phi appears squared, which removes the sign question entirely.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.
questions.question: A consultant is summarising the evidence on illiquidity risk premiums. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: It may not be possible to generate substantial illiquidity risk premiums across illiquid asset classes, but there is evidence of large illiquidity risk premiums within asset classes, where less liquid assets generally have higher returns than more liquid ones.

There is strong evidence of large illiquidity risk premiums across asset classes, but little evidence of any premium within asset classes, since securities in the same class share a common liquidity profile.
There is strong evidence of large premiums both across and within asset classes, which is the conventional view and is well supported once returns are adjusted for the reporting biases.
There is no evidence of illiquidity premiums in either dimension, which is why illiquid assets should be excluded from strategic allocations entirely.

questions.solution:
It is the conventional view that there is a premium for illiquidity. Ilmanen's analysis of 1990 to 2009 data does imply a positive relationship between the illiquidity of an asset class and its expected return. But the source cautions that asset classes cannot be completely pigeonholed by illiquidity and that the illiquidity estimates represent opinions.

| # | Objection to a premium across classes | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Illiquidity biases | Reported returns of illiquid assets are too high if using raw, unsmoothed data, and risk and correlation estimates are too low. |
| 2 | Risks beyond liquidity | Private equity, buyout funds and physical assets such as timber contain significant other risks. After adjusting for them, illiquid classes are much less attractive. |
| 3 | No market index | Private equity, hedge fund and real estate indices are not investable, so no investor actually earns the index return. |
| 4 | Reliance on manager skill | There is no way, as with tradeable index funds, to separate factor risk from manager talent. |

**Within** asset classes the picture differs: less liquid assets generally have higher returns than more liquid assets. There is currently no formal theory for why premiums exist within but not between classes; possible explanations include investors overpaying for illiquid asset classes chasing the illusion of higher returns, and firms not managing portfolios as a cohesive whole. The mispricing across classes may be due to slow-moving capital, limits to arbitrage and institutional constraints.

a.reason: Both halves in the correct direction.

b.reason: Exactly reverses the finding. It also asserts a common liquidity profile within a class, which the within-class evidence contradicts.

c.reason: States the conventional view, which the reading challenges, and misattributes the bias adjustment: correcting for biases makes the across-class case weaker, not stronger.

d.reason: Denies the within-class evidence and draws an exclusion conclusion the reading does not support.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b), exchanging across and within, which is the highest-value confusable pair in this reading and worth a Registry line: within yes, across doubtful. SCOPE ERROR at (c), which is the more seductive option because it states the conventional view that most practitioners hold and that the Ilmanen chart superficially supports.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.
questions.question: An endowment CIO is evaluating the argument that illiquid asset classes do not command a genuine premium once properly analysed. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be one of the reasons the reading gives?

options.text: Reported returns of illiquid assets are overstated if raw unsmoothed data is used, while risk and correlation estimates are understated.
Illiquid asset classes contain significant risks beyond liquidity risk, and after adjusting for those risks they become much less attractive.
Private equity, hedge fund and real estate indices are not investable, so no investor actually earns the index return and none can separate passive returns from manager alpha.
Illiquid asset classes are subject to mandatory daily valuation requirements, which force managers to crystallise paper losses and mechanically depress reported returns.

questions.solution:
Options (a), (b) and (c) are the first three objections set out in Q57 (illiquidity biases; risks beyond liquidity; no investable index, embedding the reliance-on-manager-skill point), all pointing the same way: what looks like a premium is partly a measurement artefact, partly compensation for other risks, and partly unearnable in practice.

Statement (d) inverts the evidence twice over. Illiquid assets are **not** subject to mandatory daily valuation, which is precisely why their returns are smoothed and their reported volatility understated. And if such a requirement existed it would **raise** measured volatility and reduce smoothing, which would work against the reported-return overstatement rather than depressing returns.

| Claim in (d) | What is actually the case |
|---|---|
| Mandatory daily valuation | Illiquid assets trade infrequently and are marked rarely, which is the source of the infrequent-trading bias. |
| Mechanically depresses reported returns | The documented direction is the opposite: reported returns are too high, and reported risk is too low. |

a.reason: The first objection, covering both the return and the risk direction. Not the exception.

b.reason: The second objection, with the private equity against S&P 500 finding behind it. Not the exception.

c.reason: The third and fourth objections combined: indices are not investable, and without index returns passive and active cannot be separated. Not the exception.

d.reason: No such requirement exists, and the stated effect runs opposite to the documented biases. This is the exception.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (d) on both the valuation practice and the direction of the resulting bias, which is a double inversion and therefore easier to catch once either half is checked. The anchor: illiquid assets are marked rarely, and rare marking makes returns look better and smoother, never worse.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.
questions.question: An investor has studied several alternative methods for capturing illiquidity risk premiums. Which of the following strategies is most likely to produce the greatest impact on portfolio performance?

options.text: Acting as a market maker for individual securities.
Choosing the most illiquid assets within an asset class, even if the asset class is generally considered to be liquid.
Allocating a portion of a portfolio to illiquid asset classes.
Using dynamic factor strategies at the aggregate portfolio level.

questions.solution:
The reasoning follows directly from Q57. Since it may not be possible to generate substantial illiquidity risk premiums **across** illiquid asset classes, but there is evidence of large premiums **within** asset classes, the highest-impact strategy is the one operating on the within dimension.

| Strategy | Dimension | Expected impact |
|---|---|---|
| Allocating to illiquid asset classes | Across classes | Limited. This is precisely the dimension where the evidence for a premium is weak. |
| Choosing the most illiquid assets within a class | Within classes | Greatest. Less liquid assets generally have higher returns than more liquid assets within a class, and the qualifier "even if the asset class is generally considered liquid" makes the strategy general. |
| Market making; dynamic factor strategies | Other | Both are discussed as ways of earning liquidity-related returns, but neither is the within-class harvest that the evidence most strongly supports. |

The practical attraction of (b) is that it avoids all four objections from Q58: the assets are still marked by observable transactions, an investable index exists for the class, the other risks are those of the class itself, and passive returns can be separated from alpha.

a.reason: Market making earns the bid-ask spread by supplying immediacy, but it is a trading business requiring infrastructure and capital rather than a portfolio allocation strategy.

b.reason: Operates on the within-class dimension where the evidence for large premiums is strongest.

c.reason: Operates on the across-class dimension, which is exactly where the reading doubts a substantial premium exists.

d.reason: Dynamic factor strategies at the aggregate level address factor timing rather than the illiquidity premium, and they do not exploit the within-class liquidity spread.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP at (c), which is the intuitive answer and the one most practitioners would give, since allocating to alternatives is the standard institutional response to a perceived illiquidity premium. It is the wrong dimension. The item is a direct test of whether the across-versus-within finding has been internalised as an action rather than merely recalled as a fact.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio, including the impact on rebalancing and trading and on optimizing the proportion of illiquid assets.
questions.question: Portfolio choice models that include illiquid assets must handle two aspects of illiquidity. Which of the following identifies them, and correctly describes the limitation of the transaction-cost approach?

options.text: Long time horizons between trades and large transaction costs; the limitation of transaction-cost models is that they assume an asset will always trade if the counterparty pays the cost, which is untrue in private equity, infrastructure, real estate and timber markets where a buyer may not be found quickly or at all.

Long time horizons between trades and large transaction costs; transaction-cost models handle both adequately, since a sufficiently large assumed cost is economically equivalent to an inability to trade.
High volatility and low correlation with liquid assets; the limitation is that transaction-cost models understate the diversification benefit of illiquid holdings.
Long time horizons between trades and large transaction costs; the limitation applies only during periods of market stress, since in normal conditions a buyer can always be found at some price.

questions.solution:
Portfolio choice models including illiquid assets must consider two aspects: **long time horizons between trades**, meaning infrequent trading, and **large transaction costs**.

| Assumption of transaction-cost models | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| An asset will always trade if the counterparty pays the transaction cost | Untrue in private equity, infrastructure, real estate and timber markets. It may not be possible to find a buyer quickly, or a buyer may not be available at all. In periods of stress, even liquid asset classes face liquidity freezes and it becomes impossible to find buyers at any price. |

Option (b) states the very equivalence the reading denies. A high cost and an inability to transact are not the same thing. Option (d) confines the failure to stress periods, but the due diligence problem and the absence of buyers operate in **normal** conditions too; stress is when even liquid markets join them.

The consumption consequence is the vivid one: as anyone trying to sell in a period of illiquidity knows, one cannot eat illiquid assets. Only liquid assets can be consumed.

a.reason: Both aspects and the correct statement of the limitation, with the named markets.

b.reason: Asserts the equivalence the reading rejects. No finite cost substitutes for a counterparty who does not exist.

c.reason: Names the wrong two aspects. Volatility and correlation are properties of the return series; the aspects at issue are trading frequency and cost.

d.reason: Confines a permanent feature to stress periods. Buyers for infrastructure or timber can be scarce in calm markets.

trap.explanation: SCOPE ERROR at (d), restricting a general limitation to a subset of conditions, and it is the strongest distractor because stress-period liquidity freezes are genuinely mentioned in the same passage. SIBLING SWAP at (b), between an expensive trade and an impossible one. The discriminator: a transaction cost has a number, and the failure described has no number because no price clears.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio, including the impact on rebalancing and trading and on optimizing the proportion of illiquid assets.
questions.question: A consultant lists the effects of illiquidity on portfolio choice. Which of the following is LEAST accurate?

options.text: Illiquidity reduces optimal holdings, and the less frequently a liquidity event is expected to occur, the lower the allocation to the illiquid asset class.
Because investors cannot hedge against declining values when an asset cannot be traded, illiquid asset investors must consume less than liquid asset investors to offset the risk.
Illiquidity arbitrages are available and are the principal mechanism through which the illiquidity premium is captured, since an arbitrage requires only that two assets have identical cash flows.

Rebalancing illiquid assets causes allocations to vary significantly, since the investor must wait for a liquidity event, so the allocation during nonrebalancing periods can be either too high or too low relative to optimal.

questions.solution:
| Effect | Content |
|---|---|
| Reduces optimal holdings | The less frequently a liquidity event is expected to occur, the lower the allocation to the illiquid asset class. |
| Rebalancing becomes erratic | Allocations vary significantly because the investor must wait until a liquidity event arrives; the allocation can vary from too high to too low relative to optimal. |
| No hedging | Investors cannot hedge against declining values when an asset cannot be traded, so illiquid asset investors must consume less than liquid asset investors to offset the risk. |
| No arbitrage | There are **no illiquidity arbitrages**. To construct an arbitrage an asset must be **continuously traded**, and illiquid assets are not continuously traded. |
| Premium required | Due to infrequent trading, illiquid asset investors must demand an illiquidity risk premium. The more frequently the asset is traded, the lower the premium. |

Statement (c) fails on the definition of an arbitrage. Identical cash flows are not sufficient; the position must be maintainable and closable, which requires continuous trading. Without it, a price discrepancy cannot be locked in and may persist or widen indefinitely with no mechanism to force convergence.

a.reason: Accurate, and therefore not the least-accurate answer. The first effect with the correct monotonicity.

b.reason: Accurate, and therefore not the least-accurate answer. The hedging and consumption effect as stated.

c.reason: This is the least-accurate statement, which is the credited answer. There are no illiquidity arbitrages, because arbitrage requires continuous trading.

d.reason: Accurate, and therefore not the least-accurate answer. The rebalancing effect, including the two-sided deviation from optimal.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (c) on the existence of arbitrage, supported by an incomplete definition. The definitional gap is the mechanism worth naming: identical cash flows create a relative value opportunity, and only continuous tradeability converts it into an arbitrage. This connects to the limits-to-arbitrage explanation in LO 23.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio, including the impact on rebalancing and trading and on optimizing the proportion of illiquid assets.
questions.question: A board is deciding whether to include illiquid assets in its strategic allocation. Which of the following most accurately reflects the reading's assessment?

options.text: The inclusion of illiquid assets is not as simple or desirable as it might seem: studies show illiquid assets do not deliver higher risk-adjusted returns, investors face agency problems because they must rely on manager talent which is difficult to monitor, and in many firms illiquid assets are managed separately from the rest of the portfolio.

Illiquid assets should form the core of any long-horizon portfolio, since a long horizon converts illiquidity from a cost into a source of return and eliminates the agency problem through alignment of interests.

Illiquid assets deliver higher risk-adjusted returns and the only remaining concern is operational, namely the difficulty of monitoring external managers, which can be resolved through more frequent reporting.
Illiquid assets should be excluded entirely, since the absence of an across-class premium means any allocation to them destroys value.

questions.solution:
| # | Consideration | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Performance | Studies show that illiquid assets **do not** deliver higher risk-adjusted returns. |
| 2 | Agency | Investors are subject to agency problems because they must rely on the talents and skills of the manager, and it is difficult to monitor external managers. |
| 3 | Organisation | In many firms, illiquid assets are managed **separately** from the rest of the portfolio. |

The allocation decision must also account for the investor's personal circumstances, since it is influenced by different investment horizons, the lack of tradeable indices, the need to hire talented active portfolio managers, and the need to monitor them.

Option (d) overreaches in the other direction: the reading does not recommend exclusion, it recommends **modest holdings**. Option (b) inverts the agency point, since a long horizon lengthens the period over which an unmonitored manager operates and therefore worsens rather than eliminates the agency problem.

a.reason: All three considerations, framed as the qualified caution the reading gives.

b.reason: Reverses both the performance finding and the agency conclusion. A long horizon does not eliminate agency problems; it extends their duration.

c.reason: Reverses the risk-adjusted return finding and reduces the agency problem to a reporting frequency issue, when the difficulty is monitoring skill rather than obtaining data.

d.reason: Overstates the conclusion. Portfolio choice models recommend modest holdings and high demanded premiums, not exclusion.

trap.explanation: ABSOLUTE-CLAIM TRAP at (b) on "eliminates" and at (d) on "entirely", the two options sitting at opposite poles of the same axis. As in every evaluate-clause item across these documents, the correct answer is the hedged middle position that names the limitations and stops short of a categorical verdict.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM.
questions.question: A portfolio strategist is presenting the six lessons of the CAPM. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Every investor holds the same risky mean-variance efficient market portfolio but in differing proportions against the risk-free asset, and an investor with average risk aversion holds 100% of the risky portfolio, which is the tangency point of the efficient frontier and the capital allocation line.
Investors hold different risky portfolios according to their risk aversion, and only the most risk-tolerant investor holds the market portfolio.
Every investor holds the same risky portfolio in the same proportion, since the capital allocation line collapses to a single point in equilibrium.
An investor with average risk aversion holds 100% of the risk-free asset, since the market portfolio is by construction suitable only for investors with below-average risk aversion.

questions.solution:
| # | Lesson | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hold the factor | Investors continue to diversify until they hold the market portfolio, the optimal diversified portfolio. In equilibrium, demand equals supply and someone must hold the MVE portfolio. |
| 2 | Own optimal factor exposure | Every investor holds the **same** risky MVE market portfolio, but the **proportion differs**, representing various positions along the capital allocation line. |
| 3 | Average investor fully invested | An investor with average risk aversion holds **100% of the risky MVE portfolio**, the tangency point of the MVE frontier and the CAL. |
| 4 | Exposure must be rewarded | In equilibrium the CAL is the capital market line, and the risk premium depends on average risk aversion $\gamma$ and market variance. |
| 5 | Risk is beta | $\beta_i = cov(R_i,R_M)/var(R_M)$. Higher co-movements mean higher betas and higher risk premiums. |
| 6 | Valuable assets have low premiums | Low-beta assets have positive payoffs when markets perform poorly, so investors do not require high premiums to hold them. |

a.reason: Lessons 2 and 3 combined, including the tangency identification.

b.reason: Contradicts lesson 2. All investors hold the same risky portfolio; risk aversion affects only the proportion held against the risk-free asset.

c.reason: Correct that the risky portfolio is common, then removes the variation in proportions that lesson 2 establishes.

d.reason: Reverses lesson 3. The average investor is fully invested in the market portfolio, holding none of the risk-free asset.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP at (b), between differing portfolios and differing proportions, which is the single most tested idea in the CAPM and the whole content of two-fund separation. POLARITY FLIP at (d) on which asset the average investor holds fully. Carry one sentence: same portfolio, different proportion, and the average proportion is 100%.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM.
questions.question: During the 2007 to 2009 financial crisis, certain safe-haven assets such as gold and government bonds became so attractive that they had negative expected returns, meaning investors effectively paid to hold them. Which of the following best explains this within the CAPM framework?

options.text: Low-beta assets do comparatively well when markets perform poorly, offering significant diversification benefits, so they are valuable to investors, who therefore do not require high risk premiums to hold them and in extreme cases will accept negative ones.
Low-beta assets have low expected returns because their cash flows are small in absolute terms, which is unrelated to their diversification properties.
High-beta assets offer greater diversification benefits, which is why investors found them unattractive during the crisis and rotated into low-beta alternatives.
Negative expected returns are inconsistent with the CAPM under any parameterisation, so the episode is evidence that the model failed rather than an application of it.

questions.solution:
Higher betas imply **lower** diversification benefits. Investors find high betas unattractive and therefore want to be compensated with higher expected returns. Low-beta assets are valuable because they do comparatively well when markets perform poorly.

| Beta | Behaviour in bad times | Required premium |
|---|---|---|
| High | Losses during periods of low market returns | High. The asset fails when the investor most needs it. |
| Low | Comparatively good performance | Low. The asset provides insurance, which is paid for rather than paid on. |
| Sufficiently negative | Strong positive payoff exactly when needed | Negative. Investors actually paid to hold gold and government bonds during the crisis. |

The CAPM risk premium represents the reward investors receive for holding the asset in bad times. An asset that pays off in bad times is therefore not risky at all in the framework's terms, and a negative expected return is the coherent extension of that logic rather than a contradiction of it.

a.reason: Lesson 6, with the diversification mechanism and the extension to negative premiums.

b.reason: Attributes the low expected return to the size of cash flows rather than to their covariance with the market, which is the only thing the CAPM prices.

c.reason: Polarity flip. Higher betas imply lower diversification benefits, since a high-beta asset moves with the market rather than against it.

d.reason: The episode is presented as an illustration of the framework, not a refutation. A sufficiently negative beta produces a negative premium within the model.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (c) on the relation between beta and diversification benefit, which is worth checking carefully. The chain: high beta means moves with the market means little diversification means high required return. Reading it in that order makes the direction unambiguous.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM.
questions.question: A risk manager is assessing where the CAPM's assumptions break down. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: The assumptions break down especially in illiquid, inefficient markets where information may be costly and not available to all investors, and one of the simplifying assumptions is that investors have only financial wealth, whereas in reality they have unique income streams and liabilities, with liabilities often denominated in real terms and income streams risky.
The assumptions break down primarily in highly liquid markets, where the speed of price adjustment prevents the equilibrium the model requires from being established.
The model's principal shortcoming is that it assumes multiple factors when empirical evidence supports a single factor, which is why multifactor extensions have generally underperformed.
The model has no material shortcomings for valuation purposes, since any deviation from its predictions is arbitraged away by investors who can remove systematic risk.

questions.solution:
The CAPM makes several simplifying assumptions, many of which are considered overly simplistic. The assumptions break down **especially in illiquid, inefficient markets** where information may be costly and not available to all investors.

| Assumption | Reality |
|---|---|
| Investors only have financial wealth | Investors have unique income streams and liabilities. Liabilities are often denominated in real terms, and income streams are risky. |

Option (d) misstates a point made under lesson 1. Risk premiums will **not** disappear, since investors cannot use arbitrage to remove systematic risk. Idiosyncratic risk can be diversified away, and systematic risk cannot, so it must be compensated.

Option (c) reverses the model's structure entirely. The CAPM is a single-factor model in which the sole factor is the market portfolio, and the multifactor extensions exist precisely because that single factor is insufficient.

a.reason: The conditions under which the assumptions fail, and the financial-wealth assumption with its real-world counterexample.

b.reason: Reverses the condition. The assumptions hold best in liquid, efficient markets and break down in illiquid, inefficient ones.

c.reason: Reverses the model's factor structure. The CAPM has one factor, and the multifactor models discussed in the same reading are the response to its limitations.

d.reason: Contradicts the statement that investors cannot use arbitrage to remove systematic risk, which is why risk premiums persist.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b) on market conditions and at (c) on factor count, both single-word inversions of structural facts. ABSOLUTE-CLAIM TRAP at (d), which additionally inverts the model's own explanation for why premiums exist.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain how stochastic discount factors are created and apply them in the valuation of assets.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the stochastic discount factor and its relationship to the CAPM?

options.text: The SDF, also called the pricing kernel and denoted m, is a single random variable that captures all bad times across multiple factors and states; the CAPM is a special case in which m moves linearly with the market return, and modelling returns as linear is a shortcoming that the pricing kernel improves upon by allowing for nonlinearity.
The SDF is a deterministic discount rate derived from the term structure, and the CAPM is a generalisation of it that adds a market risk factor.

The SDF is a single random variable capturing bad times, and the CAPM is a special case in which m moves nonlinearly with the market return, which is why the CAPM accommodates option-like payoffs better than the pricing kernel does.
The SDF indexes good times rather than bad, so a high value of m corresponds to a state in which an additional unit of income is of low value to the investor.

questions.solution:
Multifactor models define bad times over multiple factors using the concept of a **pricing kernel**, also known as the stochastic discount factor $m$, a single variable capturing all bad times.

$$m = a + b\,R_M \quad \text{for constants } a,b; \text{ the CAPM is the special case where } m \text{ moves linearly with the market return}$$

Modelling returns as linear is a shortcoming of the CAPM, which can be improved upon by using the pricing kernel, since it allows for the assumption of **nonlinearity**.

| Interpretation | Content |
|---|---|
| SDF as marginal utility | Periods of high marginal utility arise from loss of a job, low GDP growth, low consumption relative to past consumption, or generally low economic growth. |

Option (d) inverts this interpretation. A **high** value of $m$ corresponds to **high** marginal utility, meaning a bad state in which an extra dollar is worth a great deal, not a state in which it is worth little.

a.reason: The SDF's role, the linear special case, and the nonlinearity improvement.

b.reason: The SDF is stochastic, not deterministic, and the direction of generalisation is reversed: the CAPM is the special case of the SDF model.

c.reason: Exchanges linear and nonlinear. The CAPM is the linear case, and it is the pricing kernel that accommodates nonlinearity.

d.reason: Inverts the marginal utility interpretation. High m means bad times and high marginal utility.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (c) on linearity and at (d) on the direction of the index, and SIBLING SWAP at (b) on which model generalises which. The one-line anchor: m is high when times are bad, which is why assets paying off in those states are expensive.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain how stochastic discount factors are created and apply them in the valuation of assets.
questions.question: A quantitative analyst is comparing the SDF approach to a traditional discount rate model. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: In a traditional model the price is the future cash flows discounted at a rate determined through the CAPM; in the SDF model the payoffs are discounted using m as the relevant factor, which is what gives the stochastic discount factor its name, and the asset's risk premium can be modelled with $\beta_{i,m}=cov(R_i,m)/var(m)$ multiplied by the price of bad-times risk, which carries a negative sign representing the inverse of factor risk.
The SDF model discounts payoffs using m, and the resulting beta is multiplied by a positive price of bad-times risk, since exposure to bad times must be rewarded with a positive premium.
The SDF model and the traditional discount rate model are computationally identical, since both discount cash flows at a rate derived from the CAPM.
The term "kernel" derives from the option pricing literature, where the kernel is the payoff function of the underlying derivative, and the SDF is therefore applicable only to contingent claims.

questions.solution:
| Model | Pricing mechanism |
|---|---|
| Traditional discount rate model | Price is determined by discounting future cash flows at the appropriate discount rate, determined through the CAPM. |
| SDF model | The payoffs are discounted using $m$ as the relevant factor, which explains the name stochastic discount factor. |

$$\beta_{i,m} = \frac{cov(R_i,m)}{var(m)} \quad \text{and beta is multiplied by the price of bad-times risk, which carries a negative sign}$$

The **negative sign** is the economically meaningful part and represents the inverse of factor risk. An asset whose return covaries positively with $m$ pays off when marginal utility is high, meaning in bad times, so it is a hedge and commands a **negative** premium. This is the SDF statement of the same result as lesson 6 of the CAPM.

On the terminology, the SDF is called a pricing kernel using the term kernel from **statistics**, where $m$ is estimated using the kernel estimator. This has nothing to do with derivative payoff functions.

a.reason: Both pricing mechanisms, the beta definition, and the negative sign with its interpretation.

b.reason: Sign error on the price of bad-times risk. Positive covariance with m means the asset performs well in bad times, which earns a negative premium rather than a positive one.

c.reason: Denies the distinction. The SDF model discounts using m, a random variable, rather than at a CAPM-derived rate, and accommodates nonlinearity that the CAPM cannot.

d.reason: Misattributes the etymology to option pricing. The term comes from the kernel estimator in statistics, and the SDF applies to all assets rather than only to contingent claims.

trap.explanation: SIGN ERROR at (b), and it is the most instructive distractor in this LO because the justification it offers, that exposure to bad times must be rewarded, is correct reasoning applied to the wrong quantity. An asset with positive covariance with m is insurance, and insurance costs money. Ask what the asset does when m is high before assigning the sign.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe efficient market theory and explain how markets can be inefficient.
questions.question: Regarding the definition of the efficient market hypothesis and the rational and behavioural explanations for market behaviour, the EMH suggests that:

options.text: speculative trading is costless.
active managers cannot generally beat the market.
under the behavioural explanation, losses during bad times are compensated for by high returns.
under the rational explanation, it is agents' under- or overreactions to news that generates high returns.

questions.solution:
| Claim | Content |
|---|---|
| Speculative trading is **costly** | Which is why the average investor, who holds the market portfolio, can beat the average active manager simply by saving on transaction costs. |
| Active managers cannot generally beat the market | Even if markets cannot be perfectly efficient, the EMH remains useful because it helps investors identify areas of market inefficiency that can be exploited through active management. |

| Approach | Content |
|---|---|
| Rational | Losses during bad times are compensated by high returns. |
| Behavioural | It is agents' reactions, meaning under- or overreaction, to news that generates high returns. |

Options (c) and (d) state these correctly but with the labels exchanged, which is the whole content of the item.

a.reason: Polarity flip. The EMH implies speculative trading is costly, which is the premise for the claim that the average (passive) investor beats the average active manager by saving on transaction costs.

b.reason: The EMH's central implication.

c.reason: Describes the rational explanation under the behavioural label.

d.reason: Describes the behavioural explanation under the rational label.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP at (c) and (d), a clean label exchange between two explanations stated accurately in substance, so the discrimination is entirely in the attribution. POLARITY FLIP at (a) on the cost of trading, which is a single-word inversion that also destroys the reasoning behind the EMH's most quotable consequence.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe efficient market theory and explain how markets can be inefficient.
questions.question: A financial economist is describing the Grossman and Stiglitz theory of near-efficient markets. Which of the following best captures the argument and its internal tension?

options.text: Market efficiency is in part caused by active managers searching for areas of inefficiency, which makes markets more efficient in the process; inefficiencies are found in illiquid market segments where information does not move freely and where they are difficult to profit from at scale. The assumption of costless information creates a circular argument: if information is free and prices already reflect all information there is no need to collect it, but if no one collects it, it cannot be reflected in prices.
Markets are perfectly efficient at all times, which is why active management produces no inefficiencies to exploit and no circularity arises.
Inefficiencies are concentrated in the most liquid market segments, where the volume of information flow overwhelms participants' capacity to process it.
Active managers reduce market efficiency by introducing noise, so the more active management there is, the further prices move from fundamental value.

questions.solution:
The theory holds that markets are **near-efficient**. Market efficiency is in part caused by active managers searching for areas of inefficiency, making markets more efficient in the process. Those areas are found in **illiquid market segments** where information does not move freely, and where the inefficiencies make it difficult to earn large profits.

| Step in the circular argument | Content |
|---|---|
| Premise | Information is costless and prices already reflect all information. |
| First implication | There would be no need to collect information, since it confers no advantage. |
| Second implication | But if no one collects information, then it cannot be fully reflected in asset prices, which contradicts the premise. |

The resolution is that efficiency must be an equilibrium sustained by costly effort, and it is therefore never complete.

**Wording defect flagged under the Errata Rule.** The Book 5 paraphrase states that in this theory "markets are near-efficient and information is costless", which sits awkwardly against the circularity argument that follows, since the underlying Grossman and Stiglitz result turns on information being **costly**. Under Section 0 the worked argument outranks the summary phrasing, so this document presents the circularity as the operative content and does not rely on the "costless" characterisation. Verify against the GARP original before answering an exam item that hinges on the word.

a.reason: The mechanism, the location of surviving inefficiencies, and both limbs of the circularity.

b.reason: Asserts perfect efficiency, which the theory denies. Markets are described as near-efficient.

c.reason: Polarity flip on location. Inefficiencies are expected in illiquid segments where information does not move freely, not in the most liquid ones.

d.reason: Reverses the role of active management, which is described as causing efficiency through its search for inefficiency.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (c) on where inefficiencies live and at (d) on the effect of active management. Option (d) is the more tempting of the two because noise-trader arguments are a real strand of the literature; this reading takes the opposite position, that the search for inefficiency is what removes it.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe efficient market theory and explain how markets can be inefficient.
questions.question: A manager argues that a behavioural mispricing he has identified will persist long enough to be exploited. Which of the following best reflects the reading's treatment of that question?

options.text: Perfectly rational investors provide their own capital to exploit mispricing caused by biases, but markets may have barriers to the entry of capital, including structural barriers such as certain investors being unable to take advantage of an opportunity and regulatory barriers such as minimum credit rating requirements; structural barriers allow behavioural biases to persist for a long time.
Behavioural mispricings are corrected almost immediately by rational investors, so no barrier to capital entry is material and persistence should not be assumed.
The type of bias is the decisive consideration, since some biases are self-correcting while others are not, and identifying which category applies is the manager's primary analytical task.
Regulatory barriers are the only meaningful obstacle to capital entry, since structural barriers can always be overcome by an investor willing to accept a lower expected return.

questions.solution:
The EMH has been refined to allow for imperfect information and various costs including transaction, financing and agency costs. Behavioural biases also represent inefficiencies, which have similar effects as frictions.

| Barrier | Content |
|---|---|
| Structural | Certain investors are unable to take advantage of an opportunity. These barriers allow behavioural biases to persist for a **long time**. |
| Regulatory | For example a minimum credit rating requirement on asset holdings, which prevents a class of investors from buying downgraded securities regardless of their view on value. |

The reading's closing position answers the manager's question directly: ultimately it is **not the type of bias** that matters, but whether the investor is **different from the average investor**, and whether the return opportunities are expected to **persist**.

The connection to LO 23 is direct: limits to arbitrage and institutional constraints are named there as possible explanations for why illiquidity premiums exist within asset classes but not across them, which is a structural barrier in exactly this sense.

a.reason: Both barrier types with examples, and the persistence consequence of structural barriers.

b.reason: Denies the barriers the reading names and the long persistence they permit.

c.reason: Contradicts the closing position. It is not the type of bias that matters but the investor's difference from the average investor and the persistence of the opportunity.
