The potential gain, the acquisition price less the post-announcement price, is relatively small, and there is uncertainty about whether the deal closes. Mutual funds are therefore not attracted.

**Step 2 – What the hedge fund brings**

Specialised legal and antitrust expertise to assess the likelihood of completion, and the short position in the acquirer, which generates incremental return (interest on the short proceeds, and extra profit if a competing bid lifts the target and depresses the acquirer).

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

The edge is judgement about $C$, the probability of completion. In the return formula of Section 5, $L$ is usually several times $G$, so a small error in $C$ swings the expected return sharply.

**LO:** IM-8 c: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.12 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 90, LO 90.c, Merger Arbitrage)

IM-8 • Hedge Fund Investment Strategies • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 90 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-8 c.7)

a.reason: Polarity flip: the spread is small and the outcome uncertain, which is exactly why long-only funds are not attracted.

b.reason: Polarity flip: on a break the acquirer may rise, so the short loses too; both legs lose at once.

d.reason: Scope error: the acquirer short belongs to share-for-share deals, where the target shares convert into acquirer shares; a cash offer is captured with the long target position alone.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations that may arise when implementing this strategy.
questions.question: Two hedge funds buy the bonds of a retailer that has just filed for bankruptcy. Fund 1 joins the creditor committee, supervises the workout and is prepared to go to court. Fund 2 avoids involvement and prefers distressed situations that are less complex and less time intensive to analyse and monitor. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Fund 1 is an active investor that seeks to influence the restructuring and protect its position; Fund 2 is a passive investor.
Fund 1 is an active investor, but its involvement must end if the restructuring moves out of court, because workouts are reserved for the debtor’s banks.
Fund 2 is an active investor, because choosing simpler situations is itself a way of influencing the restructuring.
Both funds are active investors, because every holder of a distressed bond automatically sits on the creditor committee.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What active investors do**

They try to influence the restructuring: they participate on a creditor committee, supervise the workout process (out of court or in court) to protect their interests, and engage in legal proceedings when that could improve their position. Fund 1 does all three.

**Step 2 – What passive investors do**

They choose not to get involved and prefer distressed investments that are less complex and less time intensive to analyse and monitor. That is Fund 2.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

This is the swap tested in option D of Workbook A24.1: a “passive” investor who sits on the committee and litigates is a contradiction.

**LO:** IM-8 d: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations that may arise when implementing this strategy. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.12 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 90, LO 90.d, Investor Approaches)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 90 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-8 d.4)

b.reason: Scope error: active investors supervise the workout whether it is an out-of-court restructuring or an in-court bankruptcy.

c.reason: Role misassignment: choosing simpler situations and staying uninvolved is the definition of passive.

d.reason: Absolute claim: committee membership is a choice of active investors, not automatic for every bondholder.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations that may arise when implementing this strategy.
questions.question: A distressed debt analyst expects that, as a struggling issuer restructures, its senior secured loans will be repaid in full while its subordinated bonds will recover little. The market currently prices both at similar discounts to face value. Which trade best exploits this view?

options.text: Buy the subordinated bonds and short the senior loans, expecting junior claims to gain relative to senior claims.
Buy the senior loans and short the subordinated bonds, expecting senior claims to appreciate relative to junior claims.
Buy both the senior loans and the subordinated bonds, since the whole capital structure trades at a discount.
Short only the equity, because a restructuring always leaves the equity worthless.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the view**

Senior claims will be repaid in full; junior claims will recover little. The market prices them alike, so the senior claim is cheap relative to the junior claim.

**Step 2 – Set the legs**

Buy the senior loans and short the subordinated bonds. As the restructuring proceeds, the senior claim should appreciate relative to the junior claim, and the spread between them should widen toward the recovery difference.

⇒ B: the capital-structure trade.

**Interpretation**

This is the structure of the NOV example one level up the ladder: long the claim that ranks first, short the claim that ranks behind it. Priority decides recovery, so priority decides the trade.

**LO:** IM-8 d: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations that may arise when implementing this strategy. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.12 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 90, LO 90.d, ways to profit)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 90 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-8 d.5)

a.reason: Legs reversed: it bets that junior claims gain on senior claims, the opposite of the analyst’s view.

c.reason: A long position in both is a bet on the whole firm’s recovery, not on the mispricing between the two claims; the subordinated leg loses under the analyst’s view.

d.reason: Absolute claim: equity is not always worthless (firms can emerge from restructuring), and a short in the equity alone does not express the senior against junior view.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations that may arise when implementing this strategy.
questions.question: A fund holds the 5% bonds of a real estate company expected to file for bankruptcy. It bought them at 30 per 100 of face value against an estimated liquidation recovery of 35, and it is short the company’s stock. Which of the following developments would most directly threaten the bond leg of the trade?

options.text: The company’s stock falls to zero in liquidation.
Restricted institutions were forced to sell the bonds before the fund bought them, depressing its entry price.
The equity holders receive nothing until the bondholders’ claims are met in full.
The court approves new debtor-in-possession financing that ranks ahead of the existing bonds.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the bond leg depends on**

Its profit comes from the liquidation recovery (estimated at 35 per 100) exceeding the price paid (30), plus any coupons received. Anything that cuts the recovery threatens the leg directly.

**Step 2 – Test each development**

New debtor-in-possession financing that ranks ahead of the existing bonds takes its share of the liquidation value first, so less is left for the bonds. Schweser lists DIP financing and new senior debt among the developments that can erode recovery values.

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

A recovery estimate is only as good as the claims ranked above it. The distressed investor must watch the whole capital structure, not just its own claim, which is why the strategy needs legal and restructuring expertise.

**LO:** IM-8 d: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations that may arise when implementing this strategy. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.12 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 90, LO 90.d, Challenges, Risks, and Key Considerations)

IM-9 • Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 90 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-8 d.6)

a.reason: This is the gain on the short leg: the stock going to zero is what the equity short is for.

b.reason: Forced selling by restricted institutions is the source of the discount the fund bought at, not a threat to the recovery.

c.reason: This is the priority that the trade relies on: bondholders are paid before shareholders.

questions.loText: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds.
questions.reading: IM-9: Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure
questions.question: A consultant to a US university endowment classifies the risks of a proposed hedge fund allocation as portfolio-level or investment-level, following Stowell. Which of the following is a portfolio-level risk?

options.text: Style drift
Key person risk
Unrelated business taxable income (UBTI)
Correlation spikes

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the two lists**

Portfolio-level: benchmarking issues, survivorship bias, UBTI. Investment-level: counterparty risk, conflicts of interest, key person risk, strategy failure, style drift, regulatory changes, correlation spikes.

⇒ UBTI is the portfolio-level risk.

**Step 2 – Why UBTI matters to this investor**

An endowment is tax exempt, but debt-financed income earned through a levered fund can become taxable to it. Investing through an offshore fund (the offshore feeder of IM-9 d) can mitigate the problem.

**Interpretation**

The test for the level: does the risk come from holding hedge funds in a portfolio (a tax, a benchmark, a biased database), or from how one fund is run (its people, its counterparties, its strategy)?

**LO:** IM-9 a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.a)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 a.1)

a.reason: Sibling swap: style drift, a manager leaving its stated strategy, is an investment-level risk.

b.reason: Sibling swap: dependence on one or a few individuals is an investment-level risk.

d.reason: Sibling swap: correlation spikes, strategies moving together in stress, are an investment-level risk.

questions.loText: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds.
questions.reading: IM-9: Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure
questions.question: A risk analyst summarises hedge fund leverage for an investment committee, using Stowell’s discussion and the 2020 findings of the US Treasury’s Oﬀice of Financial Research. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Most hedge fund leverage is uncollateralised borrowing, which is why leverage makes funds sensitive to liquidity shocks.
Leverage can be on-balance-sheet (direct borrowing) or off-balance-sheet (for example, derivatives), and relative value funds carried the highest average leverage in the 2020 data.
Managed futures funds carried the highest average leverage in the 2020 data, because their individual trades earn the smallest returns.
Leverage amplifies gains but not losses, because lenders are repaid only out of the fund’s profits.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The forms of leverage**

Stowell: on-balance-sheet leverage (direct borrowing) or off-balance-sheet leverage (for example, derivatives).

**Step 2 – The 2020 data**

Relative value funds carried the highest average leverage, about 3.0 times NAV; managed futures the lowest, about 1.4 times (Figure 1).

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

Relative value trades earn small, steady returns per trade, so they need leverage; that same leverage makes them vulnerable to liquidity shocks. Most hedge fund leverage is collateralised with cash or assets held by the fund.

**LO:** IM-9 a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.a, Leverage and Figure 91.2)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 a.5)

a.reason: Polarity flip: most hedge fund leverage is collateralised; true uncollateralised borrowing is rare. The sensitivity to liquidity shocks comes from leverage itself.

c.reason: Sibling swap: managed futures carried the lowest average leverage in the data.

d.reason: Polarity flip: leverage amplifies losses just as it amplifies gains; the loan must be repaid whatever the fund earns.

questions.loText: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds.
questions.reading: IM-9: Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure
questions.question: A pension fund trustee asks why short selling and limited transparency appear among the incremental risks of hedge fund investing. Which response is correct?

options.text: A short position’s loss is capped at the sale proceeds, while a long position’s loss is unlimited.
Once collateral is posted at the start of a short sale the lender cannot ask for more, so a squeeze cannot force a fund to close a short.
Hedge funds publish their positions to investors daily, so transparency risk arises only from exit gates.
Short sellers can be caught in squeezes in which forced covering pushes prices higher, and funds keep strategies secret to protect trades from crowding, which makes their risks harder to monitor.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Short selling**

A long position cannot lose more than its value; a short position’s loss is theoretically unlimited, because a price has no upper bound. In a squeeze, a heavily shorted stock rises quickly, short sellers are forced to buy to close, and the forced buying pushes the price up further.

**Step 2 – Transparency**

When a trade becomes crowded the profit disappears, so funds keep their strategies secret. Investors then find it harder to monitor risks and to check that the strategy has not shifted; gates and other liquidity limits can stop them leaving.

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

Both risks come from the hedge fund edge itself: the freedom to short creates the squeeze risk, and the arbitrage nature of many strategies creates the need for secrecy.

**LO:** IM-9 a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.a, Short Selling and Transparency)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 a.6)

a.reason: Short and long reversed: the long loss is limited; the short loss is unlimited.

b.reason: Polarity flip: short sellers must add collateral as required; that is part of how a squeeze forces covering.

c.reason: Polarity flip: hedge funds are often highly secretive; gates add to the transparency problem, they are not its only source.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds.
questions.reading: IM-9: Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure
questions.question: The CRO of a US university endowment is preparing a report for the board on the risks of investing in hedge funds and on how hedge funds are regulated and structured. Which of the following statements is correct to include in the report?

options.text: A fund holding USD 100 of stock on a USD 75 loan that sees a 10% price fall must sell USD 30 of stock to return to its target leverage, the forced-selling channel through which hedge funds can spread losses.

In a master-feeder structure, US tax-exempt investors such as pension funds invest through the onshore feeder, which keeps debt-financed income from creating unrelated business taxable income for them.
Because hedge funds can transmit losses to banks and markets, the reading recommends the strictest feasible regulation of hedge funds as the most effective way to reduce their systemic risk.
In the limited partnership, investors act as the general partners and the manager as a limited partner, and the performance fee can be taxed at capital gains rates if assets are held at least a year.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Verify the leverage spiral**

Before: stock 100, loan 75, equity 25, debt to equity 3.0x. After a 10% fall: stock 90, loan 75, equity 15, so 5.0x. To get back to 3.0x with equity of 15 the loan must fall to 45: sell 75 − 45 = 30 of stock, leaving stock 60, loan 45, equity 15.

⇒ A 10% price fall forces the sale of 30% of the original position, with no fundamental reason to sell: this is how forced selling becomes contagion.

**Interpretation**

Stowell’s two systemic channels are fire-sale contagion from a failing strategy and losses imposed on lenders and counterparties (revenue, credit and counterparty risk for banks, as in Archegos). The spiral in A is the first channel (IM-9 b, Figure 1).

**LO:** IM-9 a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. IM-9 b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk. IM-9 c: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds. IM-9 d: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91)

IM-9 • Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A24.2 • S2 • Aug-2026 • Map #34 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 a.7)

b.reason: Sibling swap: the offshore feeder is used for non-US investors and US tax-exempt investors such as pension funds; investing through an offshore fund is the stated mitigant for UBTI.

c.reason: Absolute claim: the mitigants are conservative bank lending, lower leverage with more diversification, and reasonable regulation; excessively strict regulation can reduce the liquidity hedge funds supply as investors of last resort and may raise systemic risk.

d.reason: Role misassignment: the manager is the general partner and the investors are the limited partners. The tax clause is true (carried interest).

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk.
questions.reading: IM-9: Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure
questions.question: A financial stability analyst at a central bank is writing a briefing on how hedge funds can add to systemic risk. Which of the following best summarises the two channels identified by Stowell?

options.text: Hedge funds add to systemic risk mainly through their high fees and through the survivorship bias in their reported returns.

A failing strategy can be forced to unwind at fire-sale prices, spreading losses to other holders of similar assets, and a fund’s failure can impose large losses on the institutions that lend to it or trade with it.
Hedge funds add to systemic risk only when they are larger than the largest banks, because size is the only way losses can be transmitted.
Hedge funds add to systemic risk mainly by lending to banks, so that a fund’s failure cuts off the banks’ funding.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The activities channel**

The failure of a fund’s strategy can trigger contagion if it is forced to unwind positions at fire-sale prices: prices fall for every other holder of similar assets.

**Step 2 – The exposure channel**

Hedge funds can impose large losses on the financial institutions that lend to them or act as their counterparties (revenue, credit and counterparty risk for banks).

⇒ B states both channels.

**Interpretation**

The LO wording itself splits the two: “the activities of hedge funds” (fire sales) and “exposure to hedge funds” (banks).

**LO:** IM-9 b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.b)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 b.1)

a.reason: True facts about the wrong topic: fees and survivorship bias concern investors (IM-9 a), not the financial system.

c.reason: Absolute claim: a fund far smaller than a bank can transmit losses through fire sales and counterparty exposures, as LTCM and Archegos showed.

d.reason: Roles reversed: banks lend to hedge funds, through margin loans and derivatives, not the other way round.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk.
questions.reading: IM-9: Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure
questions.question: A prime broker’s risk manager is explaining to a new analyst why leveraged hedge funds can amplify price declines. A client fund finances its stock positions with margin loans and keeps a fixed target ratio of debt to equity. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: When prices fall the loan is unchanged while equity shrinks, so leverage rises; restoring the target requires selling stock worth a multiple of the loss, and the sales can push prices down further.
When prices fall leverage falls, because the collateral falls faster than the loan; the fund can then add to its positions.
When prices fall the fund needs to sell only an amount of stock equal to the loss on its position, so forced selling cannot exceed the market move.
Forced selling of this kind happens only when the assets’ fundamental value has fallen, so it does not spread to other markets.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What a price fall does to leverage**

The loan does not change when prices fall; the whole loss comes out of equity. Debt to equity therefore rises (3.0x to 5.0x in Figure 1).

**Step 2 – What restoring the target requires**

The permitted loan is $k$ times the reduced equity, so the fund must sell $L - kE^{'}$, which equals $k$ times the loss: at 3x, a \$10 loss forces \$30 of selling.

⇒ The forced sale is a multiple of the loss, and the selling itself can push prices lower and start the cycle again.

**Interpretation**

The selling is driven by the leverage constraint, not by any change in the assets’ fundamental value, which is exactly why it spreads to other holders and to otherwise unrelated assets.

**LO:** IM-9 b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.b, Figure 91.3)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 b.2)

b.reason: Polarity flip: leverage rises after a fall, because equity absorbs the whole loss while the loan stays put.

c.reason: Intermediate result: selling only the amount of the loss (\$10 in the example) leaves leverage at 65/15 = 4.3x, above the target.

d.reason: Polarity flip: forced selling happens for no fundamental reason; that is what makes it contagious.

questions.loText: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk.

questions.question: After the 2021 collapse of Archegos Capital, the CRO of a global bank reviews the bank’s exposure to hedge fund clients. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Archegos was a hedge fund that defaulted on exchange-traded futures, so its lesson concerns clearinghouses rather than bank exposure.

Archegos was a family oﬀice, but its total return swaps created exposures resembling those of a highly leveraged hedge fund; Credit Suisse lost about USD 5 billion and other banks about USD 5 billion more.
Revenue risk arises only when a hedge fund client defaults, whereas counterparty risk can arise even if no client defaults.
Because the bank’s margin loans are collateralised, its only exposure to hedge fund clients is the loss of fee income.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What Archegos was**

A family oﬀice, not a hedge fund. Its total return swaps gave it exposures that closely resembled those of a highly leveraged hedge fund.

**Step 2 – What it cost**

Credit Suisse lost about USD 5 billion and other banks about USD 5 billion more; banks then required hedge funds to reduce leverage.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

The case is in the reading because the systemic exposure came from the structure of the trades, not from the legal form of the client. A bank that monitored only its “hedge fund” clients would have missed it.

**LO:** IM-9 b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.b, Archegos)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 b.5)

a.reason: Definition error: Archegos was a family oﬀice using total return swaps with banks; the losses fell on the banks.

c.reason: Roles reversed: revenue risk needs no default (only the loss of business); counterparty risk arises when a counterparty defaults.

d.reason: Absolute claim: collateral does not remove credit risk, and the bank also has counterparty exposure on derivatives such as swaps.

questions.loText: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk.
questions.reading: IM-9: Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure
questions.question: A risk consultant is preparing case studies on hedge fund failures and systemic risk for a bank’s board. Which of the following pairings of case and lesson is correct?

options.text: LTCM (1998): the Bank of England concluded that key intermediaries contribute far more to systemic risk than hedge funds do.
Amaranth Advisors (2006): assets that normally behave independently became highly correlated in extreme stress, showing the need to monitor liquidity and leverage.
Amaranth Advisors (2006): its failure settled the debate by showing that hedge funds are the main source of systemic risk.
LTCM (1998): the need to monitor liquidity and leverage, because assets that typically behave independently can become highly correlated in extreme stress.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – LTCM**

The 1998 failure underscored the importance of monitoring liquidity and leverage, and showed that assets that typically behave independently can become highly correlated in extreme stress. **Step 2 – Amaranth**

The 2006 failure raised the question of how systemic hedge funds are. The Bank of England concluded that key intermediaries contribute far more to systemic risk than hedge funds; critics disagree, pointing to leverage and nonlinear strategies.

⇒ D is the correct pairing.

**Interpretation**

Two cases, two verdicts: LTCM is the warning about leverage and correlation; Amaranth produced the Bank of England’s view that the intermediaries, not the hedge funds, are the bigger systemic risk.

**LO:** IM-9 b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.b)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 b.6)

a.reason: Case swap: the Bank of England’s conclusion followed Amaranth.

b.reason: Case swap: the correlation-in-stress lesson is LTCM’s.

c.reason: Polarity flip and absolute claim: the Bank of England reached the opposite view, and the debate is not settled.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds.
questions.reading: IM-9: Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure
questions.question: A securities regulator’s policy paper groups its hedge fund objectives under the three high-level concerns identified in the reading. Which of the following correctly matches each concern with the way it is addressed?

options.text: Investor protection: limiting leverage; market integrity: restricting participation to sophisticated investors; financial stability: monitoring insider trading.

Investor protection: restricting participation to investors presumed sophisticated enough to evaluate the risks; market integrity: the same insider-trading rules and enforcement as other markets; financial stability: limiting leverage and requiring timely, accurate posting of collateral.
Investor protection: mandatory central clearing; market integrity: Form PF filings; financial stability: a ban on short selling.
Investor protection: registration under the Investment Company Act of 1940; market integrity: caps on performance fees; financial stability: a cap on the number of investors.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Investor protection**

The worry is fraud; the tool is restricting participation to investors presumed sophisticated enough to evaluate hedge fund risks.

**Step 2 – Market integrity and financial stability**

Market integrity: insider trading, policed with the same rules and enforcement as the rest of the markets. Financial stability: limiting leverage and requiring timely and accurate posting of collateral.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

Each concern has its natural tool: who may invest (protection), how trading is policed (integrity), how much leverage and collateral (stability). The distractors shuffle the tools.

**LO:** IM-9 c: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.c, Regulatory Objectives)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 c.1)

a.reason: Tools swapped: leverage limits serve financial stability; restricting participation serves investor protection; insider-trading rules serve market integrity.

c.reason: True facts about the wrong concerns: central clearing and Form PF are stability and monitoring tools, and short selling is restricted (in China, to 50 names), not banned, in the reading.

d.reason: Polarity flip: hedge funds avoid ’40 Act registration through exemptions; that registration is what they are structured to stay outside.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds.
questions.reading: IM-9: Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure
questions.question: The general counsel of a US hedge fund is reviewing how the fund stays outside the Investment Company Act of 1940 and the related US rules. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A fund relying on Section 3(c)(1) may accept any number of investors, provided each is a qualified purchaser.
Under Regulation D, a fund sold by private placement may accept any number of nonaccredited investors, provided it does not advertise.

A fund relying on Section 3(c)(7) is limited to qualified purchasers (individuals with more than USD 5 million in investment assets) and must register under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 if it has 500 or more investors.
To stay outside ERISA, a fund must keep benefit-plan investors above 25% of total fund assets.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The two ’40 Act exemptions**

Section 3(c)(1): fewer than 100 investors. Section 3(c)(7): only qualified purchasers (individuals with more than USD 5 million in investment assets), but 500 or more investors trigger registration under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

⇒ C is correct.

**Step 2 – Regulation D and ERISA**

Reg D allows only accredited investors, with Rule 506 permitting up to 35 nonaccredited investors. Funds stay outside ERISA by keeping benefit-plan participation below 25% of fund assets.

**Interpretation**

Every number here is a ceiling the fund is organised to stay under, which is why IM-9 d reads the structure as a set of constraints.

**LO:** IM-9 c: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.c, U.S. Regulatory Framework)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 c.4)

a.reason: Sibling swap: 3(c)(1) is the fewer-than-100-investors exemption; the qualified purchaser test belongs to 3(c)(7).

b.reason: Absolute claim: Rule 506 permits up to 35 nonaccredited investors, not any number.

d.reason: Polarity flip: benefit-plan assets must stay below 25% of the fund.

questions.question: A US adviser manages USD 2 billion across several hedge funds. Before 2010 it advised fewer than 15 funds and relied on the private adviser exemption. Under the Dodd-Frank Act, which of the following best describes its obligations?

options.text: It remains exempt from SEC registration as long as it advises fewer than 15 funds.
It must register with the SEC and file Form PF annually; quarterly filing applies only to advisers below USD 150 million.
It reports to ESMA, which both interprets and enforces the rules for hedge funds marketed in the United States.
It must register with the SEC, appoint a chief compliance oﬀicer, keep records available to the SEC, face periodic examinations and file Form PF quarterly; its reports also reach the FSOC.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Registration**

Title IV eliminated the private adviser exemption, so the 15-fund threshold no longer helps. An adviser managing at least USD 150 million must register with the SEC, maintain extensive records and make them available, appoint a chief compliance oﬀicer and undergo periodic examinations. **Step 2 – Reporting**

Reports go to the SEC and the FSOC. Form PF is filed annually from USD 150 million of AUM and quarterly above USD 1.5 billion; at USD 2 billion the adviser files quarterly.

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

Dodd-Frank turned hedge fund oversight into a systemic-risk tool: the FSOC receives data on AUM, leverage, counterparty exposures and strategies.

**LO:** IM-9 c: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.a, Regulation; LO 91.c, Title IV and Form PF)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 c.5)

a.reason: Outdated: the exemption was eliminated by Title IV.

b.reason: Thresholds reversed: quarterly filing applies above USD 1.5 billion; USD 150 million is the threshold for annual filing.

c.reason: Jurisdiction swap: ESMA interprets the EU’s AIFMD, and enforcement there sits with member states; it has no role for US advisers.

questions.question: A global allocator compares hedge fund regulation in four jurisdictions. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Under the AIFMD, ESMA interprets the directive’s provisions, while enforcement remains the responsibility of the individual EU member states.
Singapore requires every hedge fund, whatever its size, to register with the Monetary Authority of Singapore and to publish audited quarterly reports.
Hong Kong regulates hedge funds under a single licence covering all activities, with no limits on marketing to potential clients.
China’s CSRC permits leverage of up to three times capital but bans short selling entirely.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The EU**

The AIFMD (2010) brought registration, leverage limits and reporting, disclosure and marketing rules. ESMA, created in 2011, interprets its provisions; enforcement remains the responsibility of the individual member states.

⇒ A is correct.

**Step 2 – Check the others**

Singapore: registration above USD 250 million, quarterly unaudited and annual audited reports. Hong Kong: a licence for each activity, and limits on marketing. China: leverage prohibited; short selling restricted to 50 CSI 300 securities.

**Interpretation**

The EU row is a who-does-what distinction: one body interprets, many enforce. That split is why enforcement emphasis differs by country (Portugal, France, Germany).

**LO:** IM-9 c: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.a, Regulation; LO 91.c, International Regulatory Approaches)

IM-9 • Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 c.6)

b.reason: Scope error: the requirement applies above USD 250 million, and the quarterly reports are unaudited (the audited report is annual).

c.reason: Polarity flip: licences are activity-specific, and the SFO places limits on marketing.

d.reason: Both halves wrong: the CSRC prohibits leverage, and short selling is restricted to 50 securities, not banned.

questions.loText: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure.
questions.reading: IM-9: Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure
questions.question: A prospective investor asks how a typical hedge fund is organised legally. Which of the following descriptions is correct?

options.text: It is a closed-end corporation: the manager owns the voting shares and investors hold notes that cannot be redeemed.
It is an open-ended limited partnership in which the investors are the general partners and the manager is a limited partner.

It is an open-ended limited partnership: the manager is the general partner and the investors are limited partners, who can enter and redeem subject to the lockups and gates in the partnership agreement.
It is a limited partnership that cannot admit new investors after launch, because the partnership agreement fixes the number of partners.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The legal form and the roles**

A limited partnership: the hedge fund manager is the general partner; the investors are the limited partners.

**Step 2 – Open-ended**

The partnership can issue new interests to incoming investors and redeem investors who want to leave, subject to the lockups and gates in the partnership agreement.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

The general partner runs the fund and earns the fees; the limited partners provide the capital and have limited liability. Lockups and gates are how an open-ended fund protects itself from redemptions it cannot meet.

**LO:** IM-9 d: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.d, Organizational and Structural Design)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 d.1)

a.reason: Wrong form: a hedge fund is typically an open-ended limited partnership, not a closed-end corporation.

b.reason: Roles swapped: the manager is the general partner and the investors are limited partners (option D of Workbook A24.2).

d.reason: Polarity flip: the fund is open-ended; it admits new investors and redeems existing ones, within the agreement’s terms.

questions.question: A manager is choosing the domicile for a new family of funds. Which of the following statements about domicile is most accurate?

options.text: An offshore domicile can reduce taxes at the fund level, but the manager is still taxed on its fees and investors on their gains in their home jurisdictions.
An offshore domicile removes all tax: neither the manager’s fees nor the investors’ gains are taxed anywhere.
Bermuda hosts the majority of offshore hedge funds, followed by the British Virgin Islands.
The main purpose of an offshore domicile is to qualify the fund for the EU Passport.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why funds choose a domicile**

To minimise taxes and reduce regulatory oversight: Delaware onshore; the Cayman Islands (55%), the British Virgin Islands (15%) and Bermuda (10%) offshore.

**Step 2 – What it cannot do**

Domicile can reduce taxes at the fund level, but managers still pay tax on the fees they earn and investors are still taxed on their gains at home.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

Domicile shifts where the fund itself is taxed; it does not make the people behind it tax free. Tax-exempt access is the feeders’ job (Section 3).

**LO:** IM-9 d: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.d, Organizational and Structural Design)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-9 d.4)

b.reason: Absolute claim: managers and investors remain taxable.

c.reason: Ranking error: the Cayman Islands host the majority (55%), ahead of the British Virgin Islands (15%) and Bermuda (10%).

d.reason: True fact about the wrong topic: the EU Passport is a benefit of EU-domiciled funds under EU regulation, not the purpose of an offshore domicile.
