questions.question:
A transaction cost analyst at a bond fund estimates the cost of trading a cohort of similar corporate bonds from the following recent trades. Each cost is the implementation shortfall against an intraday pre-trade benchmark.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade size (USD million) | 0.05 | 0.10 | 0.20 | 0.50 | 2.00 | 8.00 |
| Cost (basis points) | 90 | 70 | 55 | 40 | 22 | 12 |

Following best practice for estimating transaction costs, which of the following is closest to the cohort’s estimated cost?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The rule**

When estimating transaction costs, weight observations by the dollar amount traded, to offset the large number of small odd-lot trades.

**Step 2 – Dollar-weighted cost**

$\sum\text{size} \times\text{cost} = 0.05(90) + 0.10(70) + 0.20(55) + 0.50(40) + 2.00(22) + 8.00(12) = 182.5$

$\frac{182.5}{10.85} = 16.8$ bp

**Interpretation**

The four trades of USD 0.5 million or less are two-thirds of the observations but under 8% of the dollars traded. An equally weighted average lets them dominate and nearly triples the estimate.

**LO:** IM-16 c: Describe and apply different approaches to model asset liquidity, including an approach to modeling infrequently traded bonds and the t-cost model to calculate transaction costs for corporate bonds. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 98, LO 98.c, Transaction Cost Modeling for Corporate Bonds (regression weighting) IM-16 • Liquidity Risk Management • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 98 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-16 c.10)

a.reason: Dropped the small trades instead of weighting them: (44 + 96)/10 = 14.0.

c.reason: Divided the dollar-weighted sum by the number of trades instead of the total size: 182.5/6 = 30.4.

d.reason: Equally weighted average: 289/6 = 48.2, the bias the rule exists to remove.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed.
questions.question: A fund’s board asks why its legal, operations, risk management and trading teams spend time on “break glass” testing of extraordinary liquidity measures that the fund has never used. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: Extraordinary measures are the fund’s first response to any redemption request, so they must be exercised every day.
Testing is needed only by the legal team, because the measures are regulatory permissions rather than operational processes.
Advance planning is the most effective defense, but extraordinary measures, though rarely invoked, may be needed at short notice, so each must be ready to activate quickly.
Once a regulator has permitted a measure it can be activated immediately without preparation, so testing adds little value.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The order of defenses**

Advance planning is the most effective way to manage unexpected redemptions; extraordinary measures apply when ordinary tools are insuﬀicient.

**Step 2 – Why test them**

They are rarely invoked but may be needed on short notice, so legal, operations, risk management and trading teams conduct break-glass testing to be able to activate each one quickly.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

The test is cross-functional because each measure touches legal permissions, operational systems (transfer of assets in kind, NAV adjustments) and trading.

**LO:** IM-16 d: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 98, LO 98.d; Golub (ed.), BlackRock’s Guide to Fixed-Income Risk Management, Ch.7

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 98 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-16 d.1)

a.reason: Polarity flip: extraordinary measures are rare, not the first response.

b.reason: Scope error: operations, risk and trading teams are part of the testing.

d.reason: A permission is not readiness; the measures may be needed at short notice.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed.
questions.question: A US bond mutual fund receives a redemption request for 12% of its assets from a single large pension plan during a stressed market. The fund wants to avoid selling bonds into the market. Which of the following statements about meeting the request with an in-kind redemption is correct?

options.text: It is not permitted for US funds, which can meet a request of this size only by gating or by suspending redemptions.
It transfers specific bonds directly to the pension plan and avoids a sale; it is permitted, but practical mainly for certain assets and large institutional investors.
It is the preferred tool for retail investors, because small accounts can easily receive individual bonds through standard brokerage systems.
It shifts the transaction costs of the redemption onto the remaining shareholders by adjusting the fund’s net asset value.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What an in-kind redemption is**

Specific assets are transferred directly to the redeeming investor, so the fund does not have to sell them.

**Step 2 – When it is allowed and practical**

It is permitted by regulation, but used only for certain asset types and mostly with large institutional investors, because it relies on specialized electronic transfer systems. A pension plan redeeming 12% is the textbook case.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

It solves the fund’s problem without a fire sale, but only because the redeeming investor can receive and hold the bonds.

**LO:** IM-16 d: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 98, LO 98.d, in-kind redemptions

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 98 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-16 d.3)

a.reason: In-kind redemptions are permitted; and gates are not allowed for US funds.

c.reason: Reverses the practice: it suits large institutions, not retail accounts.

d.reason: Describes swing pricing, and even that moves costs onto transacting investors, not remaining ones.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed.
questions.question: A risk manager compares the price-based mechanisms available to funds in different regimes. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Swing pricing adjusts the NAV when net flows pass a threshold, so transacting investors bear the trading costs; it is common in UCITS funds, and PRVs serve US collective trust funds.
Swing pricing passes the trading costs of large redemptions to the remaining shareholders, which increases the incentive for investors to run.
Swing pricing is widely used by US mutual funds under SEC rules, while UCITS funds rely on purchase redemption values instead.
Price mechanisms limit redemptions to a fixed share of fund assets, such as 10%, until market conditions recover.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – How swing pricing works**

The NAV is adjusted when net flows exceed a threshold, so the costs of trading are absorbed by the transacting investors rather than the remaining shareholders. Raising the cost of rapid exits reduces the incentive to run.

**Step 2 – Where each mechanism applies**

Swing pricing is permitted and widely used for UCITS funds; the SEC does not currently allow it for mutual funds. PRVs are allowed for US collective trust funds under OCC oversight.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

Price mechanisms do not stop redemptions; they make the redeeming investor pay for the liquidity he consumes.

**LO:** IM-16 d: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 98, LO 98.d, price mechanisms

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 98 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-16 d.5)

b.reason: Polarity flip: costs move to the transacting investors, and the incentive to run falls.

c.reason: Reverses the regimes: swing pricing is the UCITS tool; PRVs are for US collective trust funds.

d.reason: Describes a gate, not a price mechanism.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed.
questions.question: A European UCITS fund and a US mutual fund both face a surge of redemption requests during a severe market dislocation. Which of the following statements about gates and suspensions is correct?

options.text: Both funds may impose a gate that limits redemptions to a set share of fund assets, such as 10%, without regulatory approval.
A suspension allows partial redemptions up to a threshold, whereas a gate halts all redemptions and is the most extreme measure.
The UCITS fund may use a gate to allow partial redemptions up to a threshold, while the US mutual fund may suspend redemptions only with explicit SEC approval.
The US mutual fund may suspend redemptions at its own discretion, because suspension is the least disruptive of the extraordinary measures.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Gates**

Partial redemptions up to a predetermined threshold (such as 10% of fund assets); they slow or prevent a run. Permitted for UCITS funds, not for US-based funds.

**Step 2 – Suspension**

A complete halt to redemptions, the most extreme measure, sometimes in investors’ long-term interest in severe stress. Not permitted for US mutual funds without explicit SEC approval.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

The two funds reach for different tools in the same crisis: the UCITS fund can gate; the US fund cannot gate and needs the SEC to suspend.

**LO:** IM-16 d: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 98, LO 98.d, gates and suspension

IM-16 • Liquidity Risk Management • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 98 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-16 d.6)

a.reason: Gates are not allowed for US funds.

b.reason: Swaps the definitions: the gate is partial, the suspension total and most extreme.

d.reason: Suspension is the most disruptive measure and needs explicit SEC approval.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests.
questions.question: During a sector-wide selloff, several peer funds suffer severe underperformance and a bond fund starts to receive unusually large redemption requests. The CIO asks what the overriding objective of the fund’s redemption management should be. Which of the following responses is most consistent with best practice?

options.text: Meet the redemptions at the lowest possible transaction cost, since redeeming investors are the only group affected by how the fund raises cash.
Treat redeeming, subscribing and remaining investors fairly, recognizing that peer underperformance can spread by contagion and that stressed markets bring large, correlated redemptions.
Delay all redemptions until markets normalize, since the investors who remain in the fund take priority over those who redeem.
Disregard the peer funds’ performance, since large outflows are driven only by the fund’s own performance and reputation.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The drivers at work**

Severe underperformance by peer funds can create contagion, and stressed markets can produce large and highly correlated redemption requests.

**Step 2 – The objective**

Manage redemptions so that all three groups, those redeeming, those subscribing and those remaining, are treated fairly and equitably.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

Fairness is what rules out the easy answers: the cheapest exit for leavers (A) and an indefinite delay that protects stayers (C) each favor one group.

**LO:** IM-16 e: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 98, LO 98.e; Golub (ed.), BlackRock’s Guide to Fixed-Income Risk Management, Ch.7

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 98 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-16 e.1)

a.reason: Ignores the subscribing and remaining investors, who bear the cost of how cash is raised.

c.reason: Favors the remaining investors at the expense of the redeeming ones; an indefinite delay is not the objective.

d.reason: Absolute claim: peer underperformance and macro shocks also drive outflows.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests.
questions.question: A US ’40 Act bond fund receives redemption requests that exceed its cash and highly liquid assets. Which of the following describes the next steps under a typical redemption waterfall?

options.text: Draw on short-term borrowing first, up to 50% of total fund assets, and sell less liquid holdings only if borrowing capacity is exhausted.
Sell the least liquid holdings first, so that the investors who remain keep the fund’s most liquid assets.
Make pro rata or risk-constant sales of less liquid holdings so the portfolio keeps about the same risk profile, then use short-term borrowing as the final layer, within 33.3% of total fund assets.
Impose a gate limiting redemptions to 10% of fund assets, since ’40 Act funds must gate redemptions before selling any assets.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Layer 2**

When requests exceed cash and highly liquid assets, sell less liquid holdings pro rata or risk-constant, so the remaining portfolio keeps approximately the same risk profile.

**Step 2 – Layer 3**

Short-term borrowing (reverse repos, overdrafts, lines of credit) is the final option, within the ’40 Act limit of 33.3% of total fund assets.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

The order protects the remaining investors: cash first, then sales that keep the portfolio’s shape, and leverage only at the end.

**LO:** IM-16 e: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 98, LO 98.e, redemption waterfall

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 98 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-16 e.2)

a.reason: Wrong order and wrong limit: borrowing is the last layer, capped at 33.3%.

b.reason: Selling the least liquid first is not the waterfall’s rule; Layer 2 keeps the risk profile constant.

d.reason: Gates are a UCITS tool and are not permitted for US funds (IM-16 d).

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests.
questions.question: A risk manager at a US bond fund is extending the fund’s redemption model with stress testing. Which of the following approaches is most consistent with best practice?

options.text: Apply stress scenarios to fund assets, redemption volumes, ADV assumptions and transaction costs, and consider investor concentration, past redemption events and the effect of any gates.
Stress only the fund’s asset prices, since redemption volumes depend on investors and cannot meaningfully be stressed.
Replace the redemption model with stress testing, since historical redemption data lose all value once stress scenarios are run.
Stress transaction costs only, since ADV assumptions and redemption volumes stay stable when markets are stressed.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What to stress**

Fund assets, redemption volumes, ADV assumptions and transaction costs.

**Step 2 – What else to consider**

Investor concentration, relevant historical redemption events and the potential effects of any gates in place.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

In a stress, both sides move together: redemptions rise while ADV falls and transaction costs widen, so a stress test that moves only one input understates the problem.

**LO:** IM-16 e: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 98, LO 98.e, stress testing

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 98 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-16 e.3)

b.reason: Scope error: redemption volumes are a core stress input.

c.reason: Stress testing extends redemption modeling; it does not replace it.

d.reason: Polarity flip: ADV and redemption volumes are exactly what change in stressed markets.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests.
questions.question: A fund’s risk team wants to improve its historical redemption-at-risk (HRaR) model, which uses the 99th-percentile five-day redemption over the fund’s life. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Large outflows are driven only by systemic factors, so a model that uses market returns alone captures redemption risk fully.
Large outflows usually mix systemic and idiosyncratic factors, so machine learning can help estimate an upper bound on redemptions, though data quality and availability remain obstacles.
Machine learning removes the need for fund flow data, because it infers redemptions directly from macroeconomic variables.
The HRaR model is most reliable for new and fast-growing funds, because their recent inflows give a clean record of investor behavior.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What drives large outflows**

Usually a combination of systemic factors (sector-wide disruptions, macroeconomic shocks) and idiosyncratic factors (investor behavior, peer performance, cash needs, event-driven risks).

**Step 2 – What machine learning adds**

It can handle many factors and nonlinear relationships and estimate an upper bound on likely redemptions over a horizon. Data availability and quality remain significant obstacles.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

Machine learning widens the set of drivers the model can use; it does not cure the HRaR’s data problems.

**LO:** IM-16 e: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 98, LO 98.e, Modeling Redemption-at-Risk

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 98 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-16 e.5)

a.reason: Absolute claim: idiosyncratic factors matter too.

c.reason: Machine learning still needs flow data; data availability is its main obstacle.

d.reason: Polarity flip: new and fast-growing funds are where HRaR is weakest, because they lack meaningful outflows.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.
questions.question: The CIO of a Gulf sovereign wealth fund shows the board Ilmanen’s chart, on which venture capital, the least liquid asset class, earned about 16% to 17% a year from 1990 to 2009, against a little over 4% for cash and public equities. The fund’s head of risk is asked to explain why Ang doubts that the chart shows an illiquidity risk premium across asset classes. Which of the following points is correct for the head of risk to make?

options.text: The illiquid asset class indexes on the chart, such as NCREIF, are investable, so the chart understates what an investor could have earned from them.
Reported returns of the illiquid classes are overstated and their risks understated by data biases, and these classes carry significant risks other than illiquidity.
Within asset classes, less liquid securities earn lower returns than more liquid ones, so illiquidity cannot command a premium anywhere.
Venture capital returns can be split cleanly into factor returns and manager alpha, and the factor part alone explains the whole return gap.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – List Ang’s four reasons**

Illiquidity biases (returns overstated, risk understated); other risks beyond illiquidity; no investable market index; manager skill cannot be separated from factor risk.

**Step 2 – Match the options**

B states the first two reasons.

⇒ B is correct.

**Interpretation**

After adjusting for risk, one study finds most investors would have done better in the S&P 500 than in a private equity portfolio. The across-class slope is mostly bias and other risk, not an illiquidity premium.

**LO:** IM-17 e: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management (2014), Ch.13, Illiquidity Risk Premiums Across Asset Classes; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 99, LO 99.e

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 99 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-17 e.3)

a.reason: Polarity flip: the indexes are not investable, so no investor earns the index return; that is one of Ang’s reasons for doubt.

c.reason: Polarity flip: within asset classes less liquid securities earn higher returns; that is where the premium is large.

d.reason: The fourth reason says the opposite: without tradeable indexes, factor returns cannot be separated from manager alpha.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.
questions.question: A fixed-income strategist at a German asset manager is preparing a note on illiquidity premiums within the bond and equity markets. Which of the following statements is correct for the note?

options.text: Newly issued on-the-run Treasury bills are less liquid than seasoned off-the-run bills and therefore trade at higher yields.
Illiquidity explains a larger share of the variation in investment-grade corporate bond yields than in high-yield bond yields.
A 1 basis point increase in a corporate bond’s bid-ask spread is associated with an increase of more than 2 basis points in its yield spread.
Estimated illiquidity premiums in equities have risen over time and are now similar for listed stocks and OTC stocks.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Treasuries**

On-the-run bills are the more liquid ones and have lower yields than off-the-run bills.

⇒ A is reversed.

**Step 2 – Corporate bonds**

Illiquidity explains 7% of the variation in investment-grade yields and 22% in junk yields, so B is reversed. A 1 bp rise in the bid-ask spread goes with a rise of more than 2 bp in the yield spread.

⇒ C is correct.

**Step 3 – Equities**

Equity illiquidity premiums have diminished over time, and they differ sharply: about 1% for listed stocks against about 20% for OTC stocks.

⇒ D is wrong on both counts.

**Interpretation**

Within-class premiums show up even in the most liquid market in the world: during 2007 to 2009 T-bonds traded more than 5% cheaper than T-notes of the same maturity.

**LO:** IM-17 e: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management (2014), Ch.13, Illiquidity Risk Premiums Within Asset Classes; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 99, LO 99.e

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 99 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-17 e.4)

a.reason: Polarity flip: on-the-run bills are more liquid and yield less.

b.reason: Number swap: illiquidity matters more for junk bonds (22%) than for investment grade (7%).

d.reason: Premiums have declined, and OTC stocks carry a much larger premium than listed stocks.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.
questions.question: An investment oﬀicer at an Australian superannuation fund is considering supplying liquidity in the secondary markets for private equity and hedge fund stakes. Which of the following statements about these markets is correct?

options.text: Secondary buyouts, in which private equity funds sell portfolio companies to each other, allow limited partners to exit the private equity fund itself.
Because hedge fund investors can usually redeem at set dates, secondary discounts on hedge fund stakes have been much smaller than on private equity stakes.
Discounts on private equity secondaries have stayed close to 20% through the cycle, including during the 2007 to 2009 financial crisis.
Buying stakes from distressed sellers at a discount is a passive allocation to illiquid asset classes, the route Ang ranks as having the greatest impact.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Secondary buyouts**

PE funds trade portfolio companies with each other (about 15% of buyout deals in 2005). That lets a fund exit a deal, not an LP exit the fund.

⇒ A is wrong.

**Step 2 – LP stakes in PE funds**

Discounts were 30% to 50% in the 1990s, fell below 20% in the early 2000s and widened again in the crisis; Harvard faced about 50% in 2008.

⇒ C is wrong.

**Step 3 – Hedge fund stakes**

Investors can redeem at set dates, so secondary discounts averaged 6% to 8% in the crisis, and some closed funds traded at a premium.

⇒ B is correct.

**Interpretation**

Buying stakes at a discount from forced sellers is market making (route 3). Large owners such as sovereign wealth funds and pension funds are natural suppliers of this liquidity.

**LO:** IM-17 e: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management (2014), Ch.13, Secondary Markets for Private Equity and Hedge Funds; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 99, LO 99.e

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 99 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-17 e.6)

a.reason: Scope error: deal, not fund.

c.reason: Discounts were far from stable; they widened sharply in the crisis.

d.reason: Sibling swap: buying from distressed sellers is market making, not passive allocation; and the route with the greatest impact is dynamic factor strategies.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio, including the impact on rebalancing and trading and on optimizing the proportion of illiquid assets.
questions.question: A quantitative strategist at a Swiss foundation extends the foundation’s asset allocation model to include private real estate by adding proportional transaction costs, in the spirit of Constantinides. A member of the investment committee asks what this change does and does not capture. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: With transaction costs, the model rebalances continuously to the target weight, but the target weight itself falls in proportion to the cost.
With transaction costs, the model leaves a wide no-trade region around the target weight and trades only when the holding moves outside it.
Because the model lets the foundation trade whenever it pays the cost, it fully captures the risk that no buyer can be found for a property in a crisis.
Adding transaction costs raises the optimal real estate allocation, because a property held for many years spreads its transaction costs thinly.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What transaction costs do**

With proportional costs, rebalancing every period is too expensive. The optimal policy leaves a no-trade region around the target and trades only at its edges; with 10% costs and 35% volatility the region runs from 0% to 50% around a 25% target.

⇒ B is correct.

**Step 2 – What the model misses**

It assumes the asset can always be sold by paying the cost. For real estate, private equity, infrastructure and timber a buyer may not exist, due diligence takes time and a buyer may walk away; in a crisis even liquid markets freeze.

⇒ C claims exactly what the model cannot capture.

**Interpretation**

That gap is why Ang turns to infrequent-trading models (liquidity events), which produce much lower optimal holdings and higher hurdle rates than transaction-cost models.

**LO:** IM-17 f: Evaluate the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio, including the impact on rebalancing and trading and on optimizing the proportion of illiquid assets. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management (2014), Ch.13, Asset Allocation with Transaction Costs (Constantinides), as summarised in Workbook D9; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 99, LO 99.f

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 99 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-17 f.2)

a.reason: Continuous rebalancing is what transaction costs rule out.

c.reason: The model’s key weakness: paying the cost does not guarantee a counterparty.

d.reason: Costs make an asset less attractive, not more; nothing in the model raises the allocation.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio, including the impact on rebalancing and trading and on optimizing the proportion of illiquid assets.
questions.question: A risk analyst at a US public pension plan explains to the trustees how an investor should manage an illiquid asset that can be traded only when a liquidity event arrives, as in the model of Ang, Papanikolaou and Westerfield. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Between liquidity events the illiquid allocation drifts away from the optimum, and when an event arrives the investor should rebalance to a holding below the long-run average holding.
Because the illiquid asset cannot be sold, the investor can afford to consume more each period than an investor who holds only liquid assets.
If two illiquid assets are mispriced relative to each other, the investor should take very large offsetting long and short positions to capture the arbitrage.
Illiquidity makes the investor more risk-averse toward the illiquid asset but more risk-tolerant toward liquid assets, which are used to raise overall risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Between events**

The investor cannot trade, so the allocation drifts with returns and can move from too high to too low relative to the optimum (Figure 3).

**Step 2 – At an event**

Illiquid wealth is right-skewed, so the optimal trading point is below the long-run average holding.

⇒ A is correct.

**Step 3 – The other behaviours**

Unable to hedge, the investor consumes less; arbitrage needs continuous trading, so there are no infinite positions; and illiquidity raises risk aversion toward both liquid and illiquid assets.

**Interpretation**

Rebalancing below the average is the counterpart of drift: the investor resets low, knowing the holding will tend to rise again before the next chance to trade.

**LO:** IM-17 f: Evaluate the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio, including the impact on rebalancing and trading and on optimizing the proportion of illiquid assets. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management (2014), Ch.13, Asset Allocation with Infrequent Trading (Ang, Papanikolaou and Westerfield); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 99, LO 99.f

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 99 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-17 f.3)

b.reason: Polarity flip: illiquid-asset investors consume less, because they cannot hedge declines.

c.reason: There is no illiquidity arbitrage: arbitrage requires continuous trading.

d.reason: Illiquidity makes the investor more risk-averse toward liquid and illiquid assets alike.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio, including the impact on rebalancing and trading and on optimizing the proportion of illiquid assets.
questions.question: A trustee of an Indian university endowment cites Harvard’s experience in 2008 while the investment committee debates raising private equity and real assets to half of the portfolio. Which of the following lessons is consistent with Ang’s analysis?

options.text: Harvard’s losses show that every endowment should avoid illiquid assets, because studies find their risk-adjusted returns are negative for all types of investor.
Harvard’s main failing was asset-liability management: its liabilities were shorter in duration than its assets, and illiquid assets cannot be consumed.
Harvard’s problem arose because liquid assets were too large a share of its portfolio, so selling them would have depressed their prices.
A large endowment with a long horizon can rely on its size and patience alone to earn the illiquidity premium, so manager skill is secondary.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What happened**

About 55% of Harvard’s endowment was in hedge funds, private equity and real assets. It fell 22% from July to October 2008, the university needed cash for operations, and buyers of its private equity stakes asked discounts of about 50%.

**Step 2 – The lesson**

Ang calls asset-liability management Harvard’s worst failing: its liabilities were shorter in duration than its assets, and only liquid assets can be consumed.

⇒ B is correct.

**Interpretation**

For the committee the question is not whether illiquid assets are good or bad, but whether the endowment’s spending needs and its skill in selecting managers support a 50% allocation.

**LO:** IM-17 f: Evaluate the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio, including the impact on rebalancing and trading and on optimizing the proportion of illiquid assets. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management (2014), Ch.13, Liquidating Harvard, as summarised in Workbook D9; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 99, LO 99.e and 99.f

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 99 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-17 f.5)

a.reason: Absolute claim: studies find no higher risk-adjusted returns on average, not negative returns for everyone; skilled endowments can profit.

c.reason: Reversed: the problem was too little liquidity, not too much.

d.reason: Size and patience are necessary but not suﬀicient; the case for illiquid assets rests on skill.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio, including the impact on rebalancing and trading and on optimizing the proportion of illiquid assets.
questions.question: The CIO of a sovereign wealth fund proposes raising private equity from 10% to 35% of the portfolio, arguing that the fund’s size and long horizon let it harvest a large illiquidity premium. A risk consultant is asked to reply using Ang’s analysis of illiquid assets. Which of the following statements should the consultant include?

options.text: After correcting for data biases, illiquidity risk premiums are large across asset classes, while within asset classes the evidence for higher returns on less liquid securities is weak.
Of the four ways to harvest illiquidity premiums, a passive allocation to illiquid asset classes is the simplest to implement and has the greatest impact on portfolio returns.
In the Ang, Papanikolaou and Westerfield model, if liquidity events arrive on average once every ten years, the optimal holding falls to about 5% and the required illiquidity premium is about 6%.
Because illiquid wealth is right-skewed between liquidity events, the fund should rebalance its private equity holding to a level above its long-run average holding when trading is possible.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the model’s table**

Table 19.2: with continuous trading the optimal risky holding is 59%; when the average interval between liquidity events is ten years it falls to 5% (Panel A), and the investor should demand a 6.0% illiquidity premium, defined as a certainty-equivalent hurdle rate (Panel B).

⇒ C is correct. Ang adds that, given agency conflicts, capital calls and asset-liability mismatches, true hurdle rates are even higher, and most illiquid assets do not beat them.

**Interpretation**

A 35% target is far above what portfolio choice models with illiquidity risk support. “Size and patience are necessary but not suﬀicient”: the premium Harvard earned came from skill in selecting managers, not from an asset class premium.

**LO:** IM-17 e: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories. IM-17 f: Evaluate the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio, including the impact on rebalancing and trading and on optimizing the proportion of illiquid assets. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management, Ch.13 (LTR source text Ch.19), 19.5 and 19.6, Table 19.2

**Source:** Workbook D9.2 • S2, S3 • Map #48 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-17 f.6)

a.reason: Polarity flip (across versus within). Ang: “there do not seem to be significant illiquidity risk premiums across classes”, but “there are large illiquidity risk premiums within asset classes” (Treasuries, corporate bonds, equities, hedge funds, PE, real estate).

b.reason: Sibling swap. Of the four routes (passive allocation, liquidity security selection, market making, dynamic rebalancing), it is dynamic rebalancing at the aggregate level that “is simplest to implement and has the greatest impact on portfolio returns”.

d.reason: Polarity flip. Because illiquid holdings are right-skewed, the average holding exceeds the optimal rebalanced holding: “the optimal trading point of illiquid assets is lower than the long-run average holding”.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM.
questions.question: A risk analyst at a Singapore insurer is reviewing a consultant’s training slide that explains what each assumption of the CAPM contributes to the model. Which of the following statements on the slide is correct?

options.text: The CAPM assumes taxes and transaction costs are uniform across securities, so they shift every asset’s required return by the same amount.
The single-period horizon is the assumption the CAPM cannot do without, because the model fails in every period once investors have long horizons.
Homogeneous expectations ensure that every investor holds the same mean-variance eﬀicient portfolio, which in equilibrium becomes the market portfolio.
Mean-variance utility means investors dislike losses more than they like gains of the same size, which is why only market risk is priced.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What homogeneous expectations buy**

If all investors share the same means, volatilities and correlations, they all find the same mean-variance eﬀicient (maximum Sharpe ratio) portfolio. Risk aversion only sets how much of it each holds against the risk-free asset.

**Step 2 – From one MVE portfolio to the market**

In equilibrium, demand equals supply. If everyone holds the same risky portfolio, that portfolio must contain every asset in proportion to its market value.

⇒ The MVE portfolio becomes the market factor: this is GARP’s chain, so C is correct.

**Interpretation**

By itself, Ang says, homogeneous expectations is “not important”: a version of the CAPM holds with beliefs averaged across investors. Combined with short-sale limits, heterogeneous beliefs do produce deviations (IM-1 c).

**LO:** IM-1 b: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management, Ch.6 (GARP 2025 Ch.1), 1.4 CAPM (Equilibrium) and 1.6 Failures of the CAPM, assumptions 3 to 5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.1 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-1 b.3)

a.reason: Corrupted wording: the assumption is no taxes or transactions costs, not uniform ones.

b.reason: Overstatement: the single period is a minor assumption; Merton’s dynamic CAPM holds in each single period.

d.reason: Polarity flip and wrong mechanism: mean-variance utility treats gains and losses symmetrically (loss aversion is what breaks it), and only market risk is priced because idiosyncratic risk diversifies away.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.1, Eq. 1.1
questions.question: During a market crisis, the volatility of the market portfolio rises sharply while the risk aversion of the average investor is unchanged. The CIO of a Brazilian pension fund asks the risk team what the CAPM implies for the equity market. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The expected market return rises and equity prices fall at the same time, because the market risk premium is proportional to the variance of the market.
The market risk premium is unchanged, because it depends only on the risk aversion of the average investor.
The market risk premium falls, because investors move out of equities into the risk-free asset.
The market risk premium rises in proportion to market volatility, so a doubling of volatility doubles the premium.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Write the CAPM market premium**

$$E(r_{m}) - r_{f} = \bar{\gamma} \sigma^{2}_{m}$$

**Step 2 – Hold** $\bar{\gamma}$**, raise** $\sigma_{m}$

The premium rises with the square of market volatility.

⇒ The expected return on the market rises.

**Step 3 – From expected return to price**

The expected payoff is unchanged, so a higher required return means a lower price today. GARP’s example: in 2008 to 2009 volatility skyrocketed and equity prices nosedived; realized returns in 2009 and 2010 were high.

**Interpretation**

Lesson 4: the premium has an economic story, investors’ aversion to variance. Risk aversion and market variance are two separate levers, and both push the premium up. With $\bar{\gamma} = 3$, a rise in volatility from 15% to 30% takes the premium from 6.75% to 27%: four times, not two.

**LO:** IM-1 c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management, Ch.6 (GARP 2025 Ch.1), 1.4 CAPM, Lesson 4, Eq. 1.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.1, Eq. 1.1 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-1 c.4)

b.reason: Dropped term: the premium depends on market variance as well as on risk aversion.

c.reason: Polarity flip: more variance raises the premium the average investor demands to hold the market.

d.reason: Volatility for variance: the premium is proportional to $\sigma^{2}_{m}$, so doubling $\sigma_{m}$ quadruples it.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM.
questions.question: After the 2008 to 2009 financial crisis, a pension trustee argues that diversification is dead: nearly every risky asset class the fund held, from equities and high-yield bonds to hedge funds, real estate and commodities, lost money at the same time. The fund’s risk manager responds using Ang’s factor theory. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: The common losses are consistent with a multifactor model: many asset classes carried exposure to the same factors, such as volatility, growth and liquidity, so diversifying across asset-class labels did not diversify across factors.
The trustee is right: when correlations rise in a crisis, multifactor models break down, and only the CAPM’s single market factor remains a valid description of risk.
The losses show that the asset classes had no exposure to systematic factors, since factor risks would have been diversified away within each asset class.
Under the arbitrage pricing theory, common factor losses would have been arbitraged away, so the losses must reflect behavioral mispricing rather than factor risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The facts of 2008**

US large caps −37.0%, emerging equities −53.2%, high yield −26.3%, equity hedge funds −20.6%, commodities −35.7%; only cash and high-grade, mainly government, bonds rose.

**Step 2 – Read them through factor theory**

Assets are bundles of factors. Volatility was very high, growth was low, policy uncertainty was large and liquidity dried up: factors that many asset classes shared. Common exposures produce common losses.

⇒ The commonality is evidence for a multifactor model of risk, not against diversification: A.

**Interpretation**

Ang’s conclusion: diversification is not dead, but asset-class labels lulled investors into believing they were diversified when their factor exposures overlapped. Factor exposures and correlations also rise in bad times.

**LO:** IM-1 d: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management, Ch.6 (GARP 2025 Ch.1), 1.2 and 1.8 The 2008-2009 Financial Crisis (Table 1.1), 1.5 Multifactor Models

IM-2 • Factors • Vardeez: UNTIERED

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.1 (1.2, 1.5, 1.8) (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-1 d.6)

b.reason: Reverses the lesson: a single market factor cannot explain why so many classes fell together for different reasons; multiple shared factors can.

c.reason: Polarity flip: systematic factor risk is exactly what cannot be diversified away within an asset class.

d.reason: Reads “arbitrage” backwards: in the APT the factors cannot be arbitraged away, and their premiums compensate for losses like these.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Assess methods of mitigating volatility risk in a portfolio and describe challenges that arise when managing volatility risk.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.2 (2.3, Volatility)
questions.question:
The CIO of a Japanese life insurer wants to cut the equity portfolio’s exposure to volatility shocks and proposes simply raising the allocation to government bonds. A risk analyst checks the proposal against Ang’s evidence for March 1986 to December 2011:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Correlation of monthly VIX changes with stock returns | −0.39 |
| Correlation of monthly VIX changes with bond returns | 0.12 |
| Correlation of stock returns with bond returns | −0.01 |

Which assessment is most appropriate?

options.text: Bonds are a reliable volatility hedge: their returns rise almost one for one with VIX changes, so the higher allocation offsets equity losses in volatility spikes.
Bonds add to the volatility exposure rather than reduce it, because bond returns are strongly negatively correlated with VIX changes, as stock returns are.
Bonds give some but not much protection: they rise only weakly when volatility jumps, and while risk-free bonds did very well in 2008 to 2009, they did terribly with equities around 1980.
Bonds are a reliable hedge because stock and bond returns are strongly negatively correlated, so bonds rise whenever stocks fall.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the correlations**

Bond returns correlate +0.12 with VIX changes: they rise a little when volatility jumps, with under a third of the magnitude of the stock correlation (0.12/0.39 = 0.31). The stock and bond correlation, −0.01, is essentially zero.

⇒ Bonds offer “some but not much respite”.

**Step 2 – Check history**

In 2008 to 2009 risk-free bonds did very well. In the late 1970s and early 1980s bonds did terribly, as did equities.

⇒ The protection is partial and not reliable in every volatile period: C.

**Interpretation**

Holding more bonds is the cheap method; buying protection with puts or volatility swaps is the reliable one, but it costs the volatility premium. That trade-off is the assessment the LO asks for.

**LO:** IM-2 c: Assess methods of mitigating volatility risk in a portfolio and describe challenges that arise when managing volatility risk. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management, Ch.7 (GARP 2025 Ch.2), 2.3 Macro Factors, Volatility (VIX correlation table and Figure 2.2)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.2 (2.3, Volatility) (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-2 c.2)

a.reason: Magnitude error: 0.12 is a weak correlation, nothing like one for one.

b.reason: Polarity flip: the bond correlation with VIX changes is positive (+0.12), not negative like the stock correlation.

d.reason: Misread table: the stock and bond correlation is −0.01, not strongly negative.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Assess methods of mitigating volatility risk in a portfolio and describe challenges that arise when managing volatility risk.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.2 (2.3, Volatility)
questions.question: A Dutch pension fund rebalances its 60/40 equity and bond mix back to target every quarter. A trustee asks how this policy relates to volatility risk. According to Ang, which response is correct?

options.text: Rebalancing is a long volatility strategy, because selling assets after they have risen works like buying protection against a crash.
Rebalancing carries no volatility exposure, because restoring fixed weights is neutral to how volatile markets are.
Rebalancing is equivalent to selling out-of-the-money puts, because both trade option-implied volatility and earn the same premium.
Rebalancing is a short volatility strategy that earns a long-run volatility premium, but its crash losses are potentially less steep than selling options because it trades physical assets.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Rebalancing’s exposure**

Rebalancing buys what has fallen and sells what has risen. GARP: “rebalancing as a portfolio strategy is actually a short volatility strategy” that reaps a long-run volatility risk premium; the investor who does not rebalance, the average investor holding the market, is long volatility risk and loses that premium.

**Step 2 – How it differs from selling options**

Rebalancing trades physical assets, not risk-neutral (option) volatility, so it does not earn the additional derivatives premium, and its losses are potentially much less steep than those from trading volatility in derivatives markets.

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

For the trustee, the fund already carries some short-volatility exposure through its policy. That is one of the challenges of managing volatility risk: it hides in positions that are not labeled as volatility trades.

**LO:** IM-2 c: Assess methods of mitigating volatility risk in a portfolio and describe challenges that arise when managing volatility risk. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management, Ch.7 (GARP 2025 Ch.2), 2.3 Volatility (rebalancing as a short volatility strategy)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.2 (2.3, Volatility) (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-2 c.5)

a.reason: Polarity flip: rebalancing is short, not long, volatility; it loses in sustained crashes as it keeps buying the falling asset.

b.reason: Fixed weights do not make it neutral; the buy-low, sell-high pattern is a short volatility position.

c.reason: Sibling swap: selling options trades option-implied volatility and earns an extra premium that rebalancing does not.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Assess methods of mitigating volatility risk in a portfolio and describe challenges that arise when managing volatility risk.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.2 (2.3, Eq. 2.1)
questions.question: A quantitative analyst at a Swiss asset manager wants to build a valuation model that prices volatility risk through the CAPM relation $E(r_{m}) - r_{f} = \bar{\gamma}\sigma^{2}_{m}$, where $\bar{\gamma}$ is the risk aversion of the average investor. Which of the following describes the main challenge the analyst faces?

options.text: The relation between volatility and expected returns is time varying and switches sign: estimates of $\bar{\gamma}$ are positive, negative and zero, sometimes within a single study.
The relation is reliably positive in the data, but it is too small to estimate without very long samples of returns.
Stock returns and volatility changes move together in some decades and against each other in others, so the contemporaneous relation cannot be signed.
Volatility cannot be traded, unlike the other macro factors, so no market price for volatility risk can be observed.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What theory says**

$\bar{\gamma}$, the average investor’s risk aversion, is positive in theory: more variance should raise the expected market return.

**Step 2 – What the data say**

Estimates are positive, negative or zero; Glosten, Jagannathan and Runkle (1993) contains all three in the same paper, and theory shows the risk-return relation can be negative and change over time.

⇒ The relation “is time varying and switches signs and is thus very hard to pin down”: A.

**Interpretation**

What is undisputed is the contemporaneous fact: when volatility rises sharply, assets lose. That is why GARP’s practical advice is about who should sell protection, not about a precise price of volatility risk.

**LO:** IM-2 c: Assess methods of mitigating volatility risk in a portfolio and describe challenges that arise when managing volatility risk. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management, Ch.7 (GARP 2025 Ch.2), 2.3 Volatility, Eq. 2.1 and 2.4 Dynamic Factors

IM-4 • Portfolio Construction • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.2 (2.3, Eq. 2.1) (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-2 c.6)

b.reason: The estimates are not reliably positive; their sign is unstable.

c.reason: Confuses the two relations: contemporaneous stock returns and volatility changes are reliably negative (−0.39).

d.reason: Volatility is the exception among macro factors: it is traded directly, through options and volatility swaps.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the motivation for and the methods used for refining alphas in the implementation process.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.3 • S1
questions.question: A quantitative analyst reviews a set of 600 alphas for a US equity portfolio. The alphas have a mean of zero and a scale of 1.5% (information coeﬀicient 0.05, residual risk 30%), and a handful of stocks have alphas larger than 4.5% in magnitude. Following Grinold and Kahn’s procedure for trimming alpha outliers, which of the following is correct?

options.text: Every alpha beyond three times the scale should be set to zero, because any such alpha is an outlier.
Forcing the alphas into a normal distribution with the required scale is the milder alternative, because it keeps the size of each alpha.
Trimming should be carried out before neutralization, so that the scale does not need to be checked again afterwards.
Alphas found to rest on questionable data should be set to zero, and the remaining genuine alphas should be pulled in to ±4.5%.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Which alphas to examine**

Three times the scale: 3 × 1.5% = 4.5%. Every alpha beyond ±4.5% is examined, not deleted automatically.

**Step 2 – What to do with each**

“Some of these alphas depend upon questionable data and should be ignored (set to zero), while others may appear genuine. Pull in these remaining genuine alphas to three times scale in magnitude.”

⇒ Questionable: 0. Genuine: ±4.5%.

**Interpretation**

Trimming limits the “undue influence” of a few extreme forecasts without throwing away the information in genuine ones (Figure 1). It is applied with scaling as the last refinement, after neutralisation.

**LO:** IM-4 b: Evaluate the motivation for and the methods used for refining alphas in the implementation process. • **Reference:** Grinold and Kahn, Active Portfolio Management 2e, Ch.14 (GARP 2025 Ch.4), 4.3 Trim Alpha Outliers and note 2

IM-4 • Portfolio Construction • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.3 • S1 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-4 b.7)

a.reason: Absolute qualifier: only the alphas resting on questionable data are set to zero; genuine ones are capped.

b.reason: Polarity flip: forcing alphas into a normal distribution is the extreme approach, because it uses only the rankings and ignores the size of the alphas.

c.reason: Wrong order: scaling and trimming are “the final step in the process”, after neutralisation, and the extreme version requires neutrality and scale to be rechecked.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe neutralization and the different approaches used for refining alphas to be neutral.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.3 • S1
questions.question: A portfolio manager benchmarked to a large-cap index finds that her refined alphas imply a benchmark alpha of 1.6 basis points. She wants the alphas to be benchmark-neutral. Which of the following statements about benchmark neutralization is correct?

options.text: It sets the alpha of the managed portfolio to zero, so the optimizer stops taking active positions.
It subtracts each stock’s beta times the benchmark alpha from the stock’s alpha, so that the benchmark has zero alpha and the optimal portfolio has a beta of 1.
It removes the active cash position implied by the alphas, so that the portfolio stays fully invested.
It makes the optimal portfolio’s beta equal to zero, so that the portfolio carries no market risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What is set to zero**

“Benchmark neutralization means that the benchmark has 0 alpha. If our initial alphas imply an alpha for the benchmark, the neutralization process recenters the alphas to remove the benchmark alpha”: $\alpha^{'}_{n} = \alpha_{n} - \beta_{n}\alpha_{B}$.

**Step 2 – What it means for the portfolio**

“From the portfolio perspective, benchmark neutralization means that the optimal portfolio will have a beta of 1, i.e., the portfolio will not make any bet on the benchmark.”

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

With a benchmark alpha of only 1.6 basis points, as in GARP’s Table 4.2, the recentring barely moves the alphas, a sign that the optimal portfolio already had a beta close to 1.

**LO:** IM-4 c: Describe neutralization and the different approaches used for refining alphas to be neutral. • **Reference:** Grinold and Kahn, Active Portfolio Management 2e, Ch.14 (GARP 2025 Ch.4), 4.3 Benchmark- and Cash-Neutral Alphas, Table 4.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.3 • S1 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-4 c.2)

a.reason: The benchmark’s alpha, not the managed portfolio’s, is set to zero; the portfolio keeps its active bets on individual stocks.

c.reason: Sibling swap: that is cash neutralisation.

d.reason: Polarity: the beta becomes 1 (no active beta), not 0 (no market exposure).

questions.question: A manager’s multiple-factor model splits stock returns into industry, size and value factors plus a stock-specific component. Her research shows skill in forecasting the value factor and stock-specific returns, but no ability to forecast the industry or size factors. How should she neutralize her alphas?

options.text: Neutralize the alphas against the industry and size factors, so that the refined alphas carry only value-factor and stock-specific information.
Neutralize the alphas against the value factor, because the factor she forecasts is the one most likely to contain biases.
Neutralize the alphas against all three factors, so that the refined alphas carry only stock-specific information.
First forecast the industry and size factor returns, because neutralization requires a forecast for every factor in the model.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Label each factor**

Value: she can forecast it, a source of value added. Industry and size: she cannot, so they are sources of risk.

**Step 2 – Apply the rule**

A manager “does not have any ability to forecast the risk factors. Therefore, he or she should neutralize the alphas against the risk factors. The neutralized alphas will include only information on the factors the manager can forecast, along with specific asset information.”

⇒ Neutralise against industry and size; keep value and the specific part.

**Interpretation**

Neutralisation removes the bets a manager has no reason to take; it should not remove the ones her research supports. Once neutralised, the industry and size alphas are zero.

**LO:** IM-4 c: Describe neutralization and the different approaches used for refining alphas to be neutral. • **Reference:** Grinold and Kahn, Active Portfolio Management 2e, Ch.14 (GARP 2025 Ch.4), 4.3 Risk-Factor-Neutral Alphas

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.3 • S1 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-4 c.3)

b.reason: Polarity flip: the factor she can forecast is the one to keep.

c.reason: Over-neutralises: removing the value factor throws away the skill she has.

d.reason: Neutralisation needs no forecast of the factors; it exists because the manager has none.

questions.question: The investment committee of a multi-strategy manager reviews the alpha-neutralization policy proposed by its quantitative team. Which of the following proposals is consistent with Grinold and Kahn’s guidance?

options.text: Backtest the strategy with benchmark, cash, industry and factor neutralization in turn, and adopt whichever produced the best performance.
Choose either cash neutrality or benchmark neutrality, since alphas cannot be both cash-and benchmark-neutral at the same time.
Because the alphas contain no information that distinguishes one industry from another, make them industry-neutral.
Treat neutralization as uniquely defined, so that any two teams that benchmark-neutralize the same alphas will hold the same hedged portfolio.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – GARP’s guidance**

“As a general principle, we should consider a priori how to neutralize our alphas. … Do our alphas contain any information distinguishing one industry from another? If not, then industry-neutralize.”

⇒ C applies the rule directly.

**Step 2 – Check the other proposals**

“The a priori approach works better than simply trying all possibilities and choosing the best performer” (against A); “it is possible to make the alphas both cash- and benchmark-neutral” (against B); “Neutralization … isn’t uniquely defined” (against D).

**Interpretation**

The principles are tested as often as the definitions: decide in advance from what the alphas contain, expect more than one way to reach neutrality, and combine neutralisations freely.

**LO:** IM-4 c: Describe neutralization and the different approaches used for refining alphas to be neutral. • **Reference:** Grinold and Kahn, Active Portfolio Management 2e, Ch.14 (GARP 2025 Ch.4), 4.3 Neutralization

IM-12 • Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.3 • S1 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-4 c.6)

a.reason: Choosing by backtest is the “trying all possibilities” approach GARP rejects; it invites data mining.

b.reason: Cash and benchmark neutrality can be imposed together.

d.reason: Neutralisation is not uniquely defined: many portfolios can hedge out an active beta.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager.
questions.reading: IM-12: Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds
questions.topic: Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds
questions.question: A due diligence analyst at a Japanese pension fund is planning reference checks on two managers. Manager N launched her first fund eight months ago after ten years as a portfolio manager at a bank. Manager E has run the same flagship fund for fifteen years. Which plan is most consistent with the reading’s guidance on evaluating a fund’s principals?

options.text: For N, verify references from her former bank, both those on her list and those found independently; for E, focus on his motivation, his behaviour in stress periods, his communication with investors and other investors’ experiences.
For N, rely on the reference list she supplies, since a new manager has no fund investors to contact; for E, re-verify every employer since the start of his career.
For both, skip reference checks and rely on background reports, since references come from the manager’s own contacts and are biased.
For both, limit reference checks to whether the manager generated ideas or only implemented them, since that is the one question references can answer.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The new manager**

GARP: new managers need their references from previous hedge funds or banks verified, “both those that are on the manager’s reference list and those that the investor can obtain independently”. Check whether she did what she claims: trigger puller or support role, generating or implementing ideas, alone or in a group.

**Step 2 – The established manager**

Established managers do not need to be interrogated about distant employers. The dialogue moves to “motivation, behavior during crisis or stress periods, ability to communicate to investors, and experiences other investors have had”.

⇒ A applies the right emphasis to each manager.

**Interpretation**

Reference checking is a 360-degree review: if enough people say the same thing, the investor takes comfort; real differences are vetted and then raised with the manager.

**LO:** IM-12 c: Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager. • **Ref-** **erence:** Mirabile, Hedge Fund Investing 2e, Ch.12 (GARP 2025 Ch.10), 10.6 (Who Are the Principals, and Are They Trustworthy?); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 94, LO 94.c

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-12 c.6)

b.reason: Reverses both halves: the new manager’s own list is not enough, and it is the established manager who needs less digging into the distant past.

c.reason: References and background checks are complements; GARP asks investors to allocate resources to both.

d.reason: Too narrow: the role question is one part of the review; motivation, behaviour in stress and investors’ experiences matter too.

questions.loText: Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager.
questions.reading: IM-12: Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds
questions.topic: Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds
questions.question: A fund of hedge funds is completing its manager evaluation of a long/short equity manager. The analyst’s notes record four findings. Which finding should most concern the analyst?

options.text: The firm does not share equity ownership with its portfolio managers and traders and pays them a share of fund profits instead.
Every meeting so far has been with investor relations staff, and requests to meet the portfolio managers and traders have been deferred until after the subscription.
Exit triggers for positions are hard coded into the risk management system rather than left to the portfolio manager’s judgement.
The fund was soft closed last year to protect returns for existing investors and has since reopened with limited capacity.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Test the three findings that look unusual**

A: some firms do not share equity, and “one model is not necessarily better than the other”. C: GARP asks whether exit triggers are hard coded or just guidelines; hard-coded triggers are the stronger control. D: GARP asks whether the fund has ever been soft or hard closed; closing to protect returns is a way of managing the conflict between returns and asset growth.

⇒ None of A, C or D is a concern by itself.

**Step 2 – Test B**

Investors must deal directly with the actual risk takers and decision makers, not just investor relations, sales or junior staff: “if you cannot get access to the actual decision makers when you are trying to invest, it is unlikely you will have access if something goes wrong!”

⇒ Being kept away from the decision makers until the money is in is the finding that should worry the analyst.

**Interpretation**

Restricted access is also one of the Madoff red flags (IM-14 b): investors were not allowed to visit BMIS or question the strategy.

**LO:** IM-12 c: Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager. • **Refer-**

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-12 c.7)

a.reason: A legitimate compensation choice; the investor should understand it, not reject it.

c.reason: Reassuring, not alarming: hard-coded triggers limit discretion over losses.

d.reason: A soft close to protect existing investors is a sign of capacity discipline, not of trouble.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment.
questions.reading: IM-12: Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds
questions.topic: Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds
questions.question: The head of operational due diligence at a Canadian endowment explains her team’s role to the investment committee. Which description of the primary purpose of operational due diligence on a hedge fund is most accurate?

options.text: To determine whether the manager has a repeatable edge that generates alpha relative to peers following the same strategy.
To ensure investors face no significant additional risk of loss from settlement, corporate actions, theft, or breakdowns in confirmation, verification, valuation and reconciliation.
To determine whether management fees cover operating expenses, so that the firm can survive a long period of poor performance.
To confirm that the fund’s fees, lock-ups and redemption terms are in line with those of comparable funds.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the stated purpose**

GARP: the primary purpose of operational due diligence is to ensure that no significant additional risk of loss is created for investors through settlement, corporate actions, misappropriation or theft, or a breakdown in confirmation, verification, valuation and reconciliation.

⇒ B is the purpose, nearly word for word.

**Step 2 – Place the other options in their own sections**

A is the investment process (IM-12 c). C is business model risk (IM-12 f). D is “do the fund terms make sense for the strategy”, a risk management criterion (IM-12 d).

**Interpretation**

The four sections of due diligence answer four different questions. Operational due diligence asks whether the money can be lost through the plumbing, whatever the quality of the investment decisions.

**LO:** IM-12 e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. • **Reference:** Mirabile, Hedge Fund Investing 2e, Ch.12 (GARP 2025 Ch.10), 10.8; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 94, LO 94.e

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-12 e.1)

a.reason: Sibling swap: the manager’s edge is the subject of the investment process review.

c.reason: Sibling swap: the gap between management fees and expenses is a business model risk test.

d.reason: Sibling swap: comparing terms with peers belongs to the risk management review of fund terms.

questions.loText: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment.
questions.reading: IM-12: Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds
questions.topic: Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds
questions.question: During a site visit, an operational due diligence analyst at a Swiss private bank reviews the control environment of a credit hedge fund. Which of the following conclusions is most appropriate?

options.text: The fund’s detailed written procedures for trading and cash processing give strong assurance that its controls are operating effectively.
Background checks are needed only for the investment team, since operations and accounting staff are screened by the fund’s own hiring process.
Holding all of the fund’s cash and margin with a single large prime broker removes counterparty risk, since the broker is well capitalised.
An outside audit firm’s opinion that the controls are well designed and operating effectively gives more assurance than a review of the written procedures.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What written procedures can and cannot show**

Reviewing procedures “only gives investors a sense of whether the management of the hedge fund takes the whole control process seriously”. Schweser: they show “only the intention of having a strong control environment”.

⇒ A overstates their value.

**Step 2 – What gives more assurance**

GARP: some managers have an outside audit firm evaluate their procedures and controls periodically and give an opinion on whether they are well designed and operating effectively. Schweser: a proactive audit report is “usually a good sign”.

⇒ D is correct.

**Step 3 – Dismiss B and C**

Background checks extend to the COO, CFO, accounting managers and other back- and middleoﬀice staff. Cash held with one dealer is exactly the exposure that cost funds money at Lehman, MF Global and Refco.

**Interpretation**

The investor is looking for evidence that controls work every day, and that evidence is strongest when it comes from an independent party.

**LO:** IM-12 e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. • **Reference:** Mirabile, Hedge Fund Investing 2e, Ch.12 (GARP 2025 Ch.10), 10.8 (Internal Control Assessment); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 94, LO 94.e

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-12 e.4)

a.reason: Intent is not effectiveness; documents alone give little assurance.

b.reason: Too narrow: the qualifications and backgrounds of operations and accounting staff are part of the internal control review.

c.reason: Polarity flip: concentration with one prime broker creates counterparty risk; recovery after a dealer failure may be only 30 or 40%.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment.
questions.reading: IM-12: Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds
questions.topic: Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds

options.text: Rely on the website’s monthly liquidity, since the website is the most recently updated statement of the fund’s terms.
Treat the findings as red flags: reconcile the terms with the manager against the OM, and ask the law firm whether it drafted the later change and still represents the fund.
Accept the gate provision, since the law firm drafted the original documents and is therefore responsible for every later change.
Ignore the liquidity difference, since redemption terms are a business model issue rather than part of operational due diligence.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The liquidity mismatch**

The OM, subscription agreement, LPA, IMA, Form ADV and website must say the same thing at the same time; documents often drift after launch, and the OM “ultimately governs an investor’s rights and obligations”. Liquidity terms are among the items GARP singles out.

⇒ The difference must be reconciled with the manager, using the OM as the reference.

**Step 2 – The post-dated gate**

An investor “can actually check the document to see if any changes were made after the as-of date”; such changes “should be discussed with the manager immediately and with the law firm”. Managers have been known to change documents without the law firm’s knowledge, so the investor also confirms the firm is still retained.

⇒ B covers both findings.

**Interpretation**

Document review is part of operational due diligence because inconsistent or quietly amended documents are how investors end up with terms (gates, side pockets, suspensions) they never agreed to.

**LO:** IM-12 e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. • **Reference:** Mirabile, Hedge Fund Investing 2e, Ch.12 (GARP 2025 Ch.10), 10.8 (Documents and Disclosures); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 94, LO 94.e

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-12 e.5)

a.reason: The website does not govern investor rights; the OM does.

c.reason: Authorship of the original says nothing about a change made later, possibly without the law firm’s knowledge.

d.reason: Liquidity terms are part of the document consistency check in operational due diligence.
