questions.question: An operational due diligence analyst reviews the latest audited financial statements of four hedge funds. Each received an unqualified audit opinion. Which finding is consistent with the fund’s stated strategy and needs no follow-up with the manager?

options.text: A long/short equity fund that reports low and falling leverage shows interest expense that is high and has risen each year.
A buy-and-hold value fund reports large realised gains every year and only small unrealised gains.
A global macro fund reports interest income on the cash and short-term government bonds it holds.
A credit fund that lost money for the year paid its manager an incentive fee for that year.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the statements against the strategy**

GARP: “Equity funds should look very different than global macro funds or fixed-income funds.” A global macro fund “most likely has interest income earned in its income statement”.

⇒ C is consistent with the strategy.

**Step 2 – Test the other three**

A: GARP’s own example of an inconsistency: low, falling leverage cannot coexist with high, rising interest expense. B: a long-term buy-and-hold fund “should not be generating large amounts of realized gains”; it should show sizable unrealised gains or losses. D: “There should never be incentive fees earned in years when the fund lost money.”

⇒ A, B and D each call for questions to the manager, or even the auditor.

**Interpretation**

An unqualified opinion is where the review starts, not where it ends: it says the statements are fairly presented, not that they make sense for the strategy the manager describes.

**LO:** IM-12 e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. • **Refer-**

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-12 e.6)

a.reason: Interest expense contradicts the leverage the manager represents; recalculate leverage from the balance sheet.

b.reason: Large realised gains do not fit a buy-and-hold strategy.

d.reason: An incentive fee in a loss year is a red flag; recalculate the fees against the OM.

questions.question: A pension consultant is evaluating the service providers of a multi-strategy hedge fund that uses an external administrator, two prime brokers and an independent valuation agent. Which approach is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Rely on the offering memorandum’s description of each provider’s role, since contacting providers directly would breach the fund’s confidentiality.
Obtain the providers’ internal control letters and audited financial statements, and interview key contacts about their roles in execution, valuation and safeguarding assets.
Evaluate only the prime brokers, since an administrator and a valuation agent do not hold any of the fund’s assets.
Accept the providers without review if they are large, well-known firms, since their size ensures their independence from the manager.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the reading asks for**

Investors should expect the fund to make all key contacts at its service providers available, obtain the providers’ internal control letters and audited financial statements as an independent check on them, and interview them about their role in executing trades, providing technology, performing valuations or verification and safeguarding assets.

⇒ B is the full procedure.

**Step 2 – Why every provider is in scope**

Administrators and valuation agents produce the NAV and verify positions; a failure or a lack of independence there is how a reported value can be wrong even when the assets sit at a prime broker.

**Interpretation**

This is the check that would have exposed Madoff: BMIS kept execution, custody and administration in-house, so there was no independent provider to call (Workbook A24.4, in IM-14 b).

**LO:** IM-12 e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. • **Reference:** Mirabile, Hedge Fund Investing 2e, Ch.12 (GARP 2025 Ch.10), 10.8 (Service Provider Evaluation); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 94, LO 94.e

IM-13 • Private Capital Investing: Distress Symptoms and Remedies • Vardeez: UNTIERED

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-12 e.7)

a.reason: Relies on the fund’s own description; the fund is expected to make the contacts available.

c.reason: Too narrow: valuation and verification providers are part of the evaluation.

d.reason: Size is not evidence of independence or competence; the feeder funds’ large auditors relied on BMIS’s tiny auditor without checking its work.

questions.loText: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.
questions.reading: IM-13: Private Capital Investing: Distress Symptoms and Remedies
questions.topic: Private Capital Investing: Distress Symptoms and Remedies
questions.question: A credit analyst at a regional bank reviews a borrower’s latest annual report while preparing its annual credit review. Which observation is most consistent with an early warning signal of financial distress?

options.text: Revenue dipped in the first quarter, in line with the firm’s usual seasonal pattern.
The tax charge appears low relative to the earnings the firm reports.
Almost all of the year’s earnings were generated by the firm’s core operations.
The firm kept the same auditor and the same fiscal year-end as in prior years.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the early-warning questions**

The reading’s accounting questions include: are earnings generated from core operations, and does the tax charge appear low relative to reported earnings?

⇒ A tax charge that looks low against reported earnings suggests the earnings may be overstated: an early warning signal.

**Step 2 – Check the other observations**

A dip that follows the usual seasonal pattern is the kind of temporary fluctuation the analyst must separate from a permanent deterioration. Earnings from core operations, and an unchanged auditor and fiscal year-end, are the healthy answers to the reading’s questions.

**Interpretation**

The tax line is hard to inflate along with profits: when reported earnings rise but the tax charge does not, ask what kind of earnings they are.

**LO:** IM-13 a: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.a

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-13 a.2)

a.reason: A seasonal dip is a temporary fluctuation, not by itself a distress signal.

c.reason: Earnings from core operations are the reassuring answer to the first question.

d.reason: Changes of auditor or fiscal year-end are warning signs; keeping them is not.

questions.topic: Private Capital Investing: Distress Symptoms and Remedies
questions.question: A distressed-debt analyst is preparing a training note on why firms default. Which statement about performing well below expectations as a cause of financial distress is correct?

options.text: It is the most common cause of distress, and in a recession the key challenge is to judge whether the downturn itself or management’s decisions drive the deterioration.
It is a rare cause of distress, because recessions can be forecast and their effect on revenue hedged in advance.
It covers products that lose demand as preferences shift, which the reading classifies as a crisis of confidence.
In a recession, the deterioration should always be attributed to the business cycle rather than to management’s strategy.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the reading’s statement**

“Performing well below expectations. This is the most common cause of financial distress.” Its two triggers are economic downturns and uncompetitive products or services.

**Step 2 – The diagnostic challenge**

For downturns, “the key challenge is determining whether the downturn itself is driving the deterioration, or whether management decisions and strategies are the underlying cause”.

⇒ A states both points.

**Interpretation**

The diagnosis matters for the remedy: a cyclical problem may need time and liquidity; a management problem needs a new plan, and extra capital can simply give weak management more time to destroy value (IM-13 b).

**LO:** IM-13 a: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.a

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-13 a.3)

b.reason: Polarity flip: it is the most common cause, and the business cycle “is unavoidable”.

c.reason: Sibling swap: obsolete products are the second trigger of performing below expectations; a crisis of confidence is usually fraud.

d.reason: Absolute claim: the reading asks the analyst to separate the cycle from management’s decisions, not to assume the answer.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.
questions.reading: IM-13: Private Capital Investing: Distress Symptoms and Remedies
questions.topic: Private Capital Investing: Distress Symptoms and Remedies
questions.question: A distressed-debt analyst groups four troubled borrowers by the main cause of their distress. Which grouping is correct?

options.text: A roll-up of 40 regional dental practices whose expected economies of scale never materialised: performing well below expectations.
A chemicals maker facing a class action over groundwater contamination that its insurance may not cover: unexpected liabilities.
A retailer whose sales collapsed after its customers moved online: crisis of confidence.
A logistics firm whose former CFO is found to have inflated revenue for five years: unrealistic business plan.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the five families**

Leverage and business performance; unexpected liabilities (tort, contract); performing well below expectations (downturns, uncompetitive products); crisis of confidence (often fraud); unrealistic business plans (LBOs, roll-ups, too many entrants).

**Step 2 – Place each borrower**

Class action for environmental harm: a tort liability, under unexpected liabilities, often underestimated by management and possibly uninsured. Roll-up whose economies of scale never came: unrealistic business plan. Retailer losing customers to online rivals: uncompetitive products, under performing below expectations. CFO fraud: crisis of confidence.

⇒ Only B is grouped correctly.

**Interpretation**

Markets typically “assume the worst” about a tort claim and discount the firm’s securities before the award is known.

**LO:** IM-13 a: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.a

questions.question: Shortly after a manufacturer discloses that its former CFO falsified three years of revenue, a credit analyst at an insurer that holds the firm’s bonds is asked what to assess first. Which approach is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Treat only the three restated years as unreliable, since information from outside the fraud period is unaffected.
Assess how far the fraud contaminates all previously reported information, and whether it could trigger a liquidity crisis through cash balances, credit lines and loan acceleration.
Focus on whether the firm’s products remain competitive, since a crisis of confidence is mainly a problem of customer demand.
Wait for the next audited statements before acting, since market prices overreact to fraud news and then recover.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Reliability of historical information**

“Once financial fraud is uncovered, all previously reported financial information becomes suspect.” The analyst assesses the informational contagion and whether there is a practical cutoff point for reliable data.

**Step 2 – Liquidity and the likelihood of bankruptcy**

The analyst asks whether the fraud could trigger liquidity problems: cash balances, the availability of credit lines and the risk of loan acceleration.

⇒ B covers the two areas of focus the reading names.

**Interpretation**

A crisis of confidence turns a reporting problem into a funding problem: lenders who no longer trust the numbers can pull lines or accelerate loans.

**LO:** IM-13 a: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.a

IM-13 • Private Capital Investing: Distress Symptoms and Remedies • Vardeez: UNTIERED

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-13 a.6)

a.reason: Too narrow: the contagion can reach information outside the restated years; that is why a cutoff point must be found.

c.reason: Sibling swap: competitiveness belongs to performing below expectations.

d.reason: Waiting ignores the immediate liquidity question, which is the more urgent of the two.

questions.question: A distressed-debt analyst notes that a retailer’s senior bonds now trade at 45 per 100 of face value, down from 92 six months ago. Which interpretation of the debt trading level is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: The lower trading level signals that the market expects more severe distress, and it informs the analyst about which restructuring solutions are realistic.
The lower trading level signals that the market expects milder distress, because cheaper bonds make open market repurchases more attractive.
The trading level is informative only for bank loans, because bond prices mainly reflect changes in interest rates.
The trading level measures the bonds’ coupon relative to market yields and says nothing about the restructuring options.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the trading level is**

The debt trading level is the current market price of the debt relative to its full repayment value. **Step 2 – What it tells the analyst**

It “serves as an indicator of the market’s expectations about distress severity and potential restructuring options”. A fall from 92 to 45 means the market expects far less to be repaid.

⇒ A: deeper expected distress, and a guide to the realistic solutions.

**Interpretation**

The price is the market’s verdict on the stage of distress. Near full value, the problem looks like liquidity; far below it, the market is pricing in a restructuring of the claim itself.

**LO:** IM-13 b: Describe methods firms can use to remedy a financial distress situation at different stages of distress and explain the potential implications and challenges to using each method. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20 (after Moyer, 2005); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.b

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-13 b.1)

b.reason: Polarity flip: a lower price signals more severe expected distress. Cheaper bonds can make a discounted buyback attractive, but only for a firm with cash to spare.

c.reason: The reading applies the trading level to a firm’s actively traded debt; a fall from 92 to 45 is a credit signal, not a rate move.

d.reason: The trading level is a price relative to repayment value, and the reading links it directly to the restructuring options.

questions.question: A distressed industrial firm with almost no cash wants to cut its bond debt. It offers bondholders new secured notes in exchange for their existing unsecured bonds, and warns that bondholders who do not take part may end up worse off than those who do. Which method is the firm using?

options.text: A noncoercive exchange offer.
A cash tender offer.
A coercive exchange offer.
A direct purchase from bondholders.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Identify the family**

The firm lacks cash and offers new securities for its distressed debt: an exchange offer, not a cash tender or a direct purchase.

**Step 2 – Coercive or noncoercive**

Exchange offers “may be coercive, meaning participants are warned that nonparticipants may be disadvantaged”; noncoercive offers encourage participation by highlighting the opportunity’s attractiveness.

⇒ The warning makes it a coercive exchange offer.

**Interpretation**

Coercion is the firm’s answer to the holdout problem: if staying out looks worse than taking part, fewer creditors hold out (IM-13 c).

**LO:** IM-13 b: Describe methods firms can use to remedy a financial distress situation at different stages of distress and explain the potential implications and challenges to using each method. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.b

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-13 b.4)

a.reason: A noncoercive offer persuades with attractive terms, not with a warning.

b.reason: A tender offer pays cash; this firm has almost none.

d.reason: A direct purchase is a negotiated deal with individual holders, usually for cash.

questions.question: A restructuring adviser briefs the board of a distressed company on the implications of different ways to raise capital and reduce leverage. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A private equity sponsor holding more than 50% of the equity is generally positive for creditors, because the sponsor realises value only after the debt claims are satisfied.
Assets generally fetch better prices after a bankruptcy filing, so a distressed firm should delay asset sales until it has filed.
Secured financing is usually the easiest source of cash for a distressed firm, because its most valuable assets are rarely pledged.
An equity injection from new outside investors can usually be arranged faster than one from the firm’s incumbent investors.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The equity sponsor**

“A private owner with more than a 50% stake is generally positive for distressed investors. A majority equity holder realizes value only after debt claims are satisfied, which aligns incentives.”

⇒ A is correct.

**Step 2 – Test B, C and D**

Asset sales: a favourable price is “generally easier to obtain before a bankruptcy filing”. Secured financing: “often limited”, since the most valuable assets were pledged in earlier restructurings. Equity: incumbent capital “can typically be arranged quickly”, while new investors take longer because of due diligence.

⇒ B, C and D each reverse the reading.

**Interpretation**

Each method’s implication follows from timing and incentives: sell early, expect the collateral to be gone, and look to existing owners first for fast equity.

**LO:** IM-13 b: Describe methods firms can use to remedy a financial distress situation at different stages of distress and explain the potential implications and challenges to using each method. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.b

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-13 b.5)

b.reason: Polarity flip on timing: sell before filing.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the best assets are usually already pledged.

d.reason: Reversed: incumbents are faster; newcomers need time for due diligence.

questions.question: The head of risk at a global asset manager tells the board that the firm’s market-driven scenario (MDS) process is designed to meet James Surowiecki’s three criteria for good collective decisions. Which of the following correctly matches a feature of the MDS process with the criterion it satisfies?

options.text: Requiring every expert to adopt the firm’s house economic view before proposing shocks satisfies the criterion that opinions be independent.
A centralized process run by the risk management department to aggregate the ideas into a collective view satisfies the criterion of an objective aggregation mechanism.
Passing the policy shocks through a covariance matrix satisfies the criterion that each individual possess specialized knowledge not available to others.
Letting the experts settle the scenario among themselves, without the risk function, satisfies the criterion of an objective aggregation mechanism.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The three criteria**

(1) Each individual has specialized knowledge not available to others; (2) opinions are independent and not influenced by groupthink; (3) there is an objective mechanism for aggregating private views into a collective assessment.

**Step 2 – Match the MDS features**

The diverse group of professionals supplies (1). The firm’s risk management department “develops a centralized process to aggregate these ideas into a collective view”: that is (3).

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

The mapping explains why the aggregation sits with risk management rather than with any one investment team: an aggregator that has no stake in a particular view is what makes the mechanism objective.

**LO:** IM-15 a: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.a (Surowiecki, The Wisdom of Crowds)

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 97 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-15 a.2)

a.reason: Polarity flip: imposing a house view is the groupthink that the independence criterion rules out.

c.reason: Sibling swap: the covariance matrix is a statistical tool that implies the nonpolicy shocks; specialized knowledge comes from the diverse experts.

d.reason: Removing the central risk function removes the objective aggregator; a consensus reached among the experts themselves invites groupthink.

questions.question: At an investment committee meeting, the CIO of a balanced fund proposes replacing the fund’s 99% VaR limit with the loss from the firm’s Soft Brexit market-driven scenario, which he describes as “our new measure of tail loss”. Which of the following responses is most consistent with the purpose of the MDS approach?

options.text: The proposal is appropriate, because the MDS approach is designed to quantify the tail loss of a portfolio at a stated confidence level.
The proposal is appropriate, because a scenario’s P&L can be converted into an exact probability of loss without any further assumptions.
The proposal misreads the approach: MDS does not quantify tail losses or set targets; it integrates views in a structured way and prompts managers to reassess their convictions.
The proposal misreads the approach: MDS scenarios are built only from historical episodes, so they cannot inform any forward-looking decision.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the approach is for**

“The goal of the MDS approach is not to quantify tail losses or force risk managers to target specific outcomes. Instead, it is a tool for integrating insights from different perspectives in a structured way.”

**Step 2 – What it gives instead**

By quantifying returns under scenarios of varying plausibility, it encourages managers to reassess their strategic convictions and increases awareness of alternative outcomes.

⇒ The CIO’s proposal misreads the approach: C.

**Interpretation**

A scenario loss is the outcome of one coherent story, with no confidence level attached. It complements a VaR limit; it does not replace it.

**LO:** IM-15 a: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.a and LO 97.c (closing paragraph of the Brexit example)

IM-17 • Illiquid Assets • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 97 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-15 a.6)

a.reason: Purpose error: quantifying tail losses at a confidence level is what the reading says MDS is not for.

b.reason: Absolute claim: scenario z-scores give only relative probabilities; an absolute probability needs further assumptions (IM-15 b).

d.reason: Right verdict, wrong reason: MDS scenarios are forward-looking, not built only from historical episodes.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.
questions.question: The head of real estate at a Canadian pension plan unsmooths the quarterly returns of the plan’s appraisal-based property index before the annual asset allocation review. The reported series has a first-order autocorrelation of 0.70, and the properties are reappraised once a year. Which of the following statements about the unsmoothed series is correct?

options.text: Its average quarterly return will be well below the reported average, because unsmoothing restores the losses that the appraisers failed to record.
Its average quarterly return will be close to the reported average, because smoothing spreads each shock over several quarters without removing it.
A first-order AR(1) filter is suﬀicient for this index, because the annual reappraisal cycle affects the level of the index but not the lag structure of its returns.
Its volatility will be lower than the reported volatility, because the filter removes the noise that appraisal errors add to the reported returns.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What smoothing does to the level**

Each true shock is spread over several quarters but still counted in full, so the index ends where the true index ends. Summing the filter gives $\sum r_{t} = \sum r^{*}_{t} + \frac{\phi}{1-\phi}(r^{*}_{T} - r^{*}_{0})$, a single end term.

⇒ The average return is essentially unchanged: Ang’s first property.

**Step 2 – What it does to dispersion**

The filter adds noise back, so volatility rises: with $\phi= 0.70$ a pure AR(1) filter would scale it by $\sqrt{1.7/0.3} = 2.38$.

**Step 3 – What the reappraisal cycle does**

Annual reappraisals put a fourth-order lag into quarterly returns. A first-order filter misses it; Ang’s third property is that unsmoothing is an art, best done with an ARMA model and knowledge of how the market is valued.

**Interpretation**

Unsmoothing changes the path, not the destination. Individual bad quarters become much worse, which is easy to mistake for a lower mean.

**LO:** IM-17 d: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management (2014), Ch.13, Unsmoothing (three properties), as reported in Vardeez IM-17 d and Workbook D9; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 99, LO 99.d

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 99 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-17 d.4)

a.reason: Confuses deeper individual quarters with a lower mean: unsmoothing affects risk estimates, not expected returns.

c.reason: Annual reappraisal creates a fourth-order lag in quarterly data; one lag is not enough.

d.reason: Polarity flip: unsmoothing adds noise back and raises volatility.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.
questions.question:
A risk manager at a Dutch insurer presents the following statistics for a private real estate index to the investment committee. Over the same period the quarterly volatility of US equities was about 7.5%.

|  | Reported | Unsmoothed |
|---|---|---|
| First-order autocorrelation | 0.78 | close to 0 |
| Quarterly volatility | 2.25% | 6.26% |
| Correlation with the S&P 500 | 9.2% | 15.8% |
| Worst quarter (December 2008) | −8.3% | −36.3% |

Which of the following conclusions should the risk manager draw?

options.text: Real estate’s expected return was overstated by about 28 percentage points, so the index mean must be lowered before it enters the optimiser.
Real estate’s Sharpe ratio is lower on unsmoothed data, and an optimiser fed the unsmoothed statistics will allocate less to real estate.
Because the unsmoothed correlation is still below 20%, smoothing biased the volatility estimate but not the correlation estimate.
Because reported volatility is less than a third of equity volatility, real estate is a low-risk diversifier whose allocation can be raised.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the table**

Unsmoothing multiplies quarterly volatility by 6.26/2.25 = 2.8, to a level close to equities (7.5%), raises the correlation with the S&P 500 from 9.2% to 15.8%, and turns a −8.3% quarter into −36.3%.

**Step 2 – Effect on the Sharpe ratio**

The mean is unchanged by unsmoothing, so the excess return stays the same while volatility is 2.8 times larger.

⇒ The Sharpe ratio falls to about a third of its reported value.

**Step 3 – Effect on the allocation**

Higher volatility and higher correlation with equities both reduce the optimal mean-variance weight.

⇒ The optimiser allocates less to real estate on unsmoothed data.

**Interpretation**

Reported appraisal data make real estate look like a near-riskless diversifier. The committee should put unsmoothed statistics into the optimiser.

**LO:** IM-17 d: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management (2014), Ch.13, Unsmoothing (NCREIF example); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 99, LO 99.c and 99.d

**Source:** New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 99 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-17 d.5)

a.reason: The −36.3% is one quarter’s unsmoothed return, not a bias in the mean; the expected return is unchanged by unsmoothing. The 28 points is 36.3−8.3, a gap in one quarter’s return.

c.reason: The correlation rose from 9.2% to 15.8%: smoothing biases correlations downward too.

d.reason: The 2.25% is the smoothed figure. Unsmoothed, real estate volatility (6.26%) is close to that of equities.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.
questions.question: A member of the investment committee of a Canadian university endowment is reviewing a consultant’s report that relies on two data sets: an appraisal-based institutional real estate index whose quarterly returns show a first-order autocorrelation of 0.75, and a commercial database of venture capital returns to which reporting is voluntary. Which of the following statements is correct to include in the committee’s response to the consultant?

options.text: Unsmoothing the real estate index with an AR(1) filter will raise its estimated volatility, correlation and beta with equities, but will leave its estimated expected return essentially unchanged.
Survivorship bias in the venture capital database makes reported returns understate true returns, because funds that drop out of the database tend to be those with above-average returns.
Selection bias in the venture capital database, which arises because values are recorded mainly when they are high, is corrected by applying the same Geltner-Ross-Zisler unsmoothing filter.
The downward bias in the real estate index’s volatility is a small-sample problem that will disappear once the consultant uses a suﬀiciently long history of reported quarterly returns.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the autocorrelation**

A first-order autocorrelation of 0.75 signals appraisal smoothing. Infrequent trading makes “estimates of risk, volatilities, correlations, and betas” too low; unsmoothing adds noise back to recover the true returns.

**Step 2 – Apply Ang’s first property**

“Unsmoothing affects only risk estimates and not expected returns”, because smoothing spreads shocks over several periods but still counts all of them, so the first and last prices are unchanged.

⇒ A is correct. For NCREIF, volatility rose from 2.25% to 6.26% a quarter and the correlation with the S&P 500 from 9.2% to 15.8%.

**Interpretation**

The committee should ask for unsmoothed risk estimates before the real estate allocation enters a mean-variance optimiser; raw appraisal data make the asset look like a near-riskless diversifier. With $\phi= 0.75$ a pure AR(1) filter would scale the reported volatility by $\sqrt{1.75/0.25} = 2.65$.

**LO:** IM-17 c: Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets. IM-17 d: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management, Ch.13 (LTR source text Ch.19), 19.4

**Source:** Workbook D9.1 • S1 • Map #48 (Risk Management and Investment Management Workbook, Question IM-17 d.6)

b.reason: Polarity flip: survivorship bias “results from the tendency of poorly performing funds to stop reporting”, so reported returns overstate true returns.

c.reason: Sibling swap: unsmoothing corrects infrequent trading. Selection bias is addressed with Heckman (1979) selection models, which let the threshold above which returns are observed vary over time.

d.reason: Scope error: Ang states that the infrequent-observation bias “is not a ‘small sample’ problem, which goes away when our sample becomes very large; it is a ‘population’ problem”.
